Institute of Fine Arts") – enjoy international reputations,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-26) and the city has vibrant and influential grassroots [art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_Birmingham "Art of Birmingham"), [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music_of_Birmingham "Popular music of Birmingham"), [literary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literature_of_Birmingham "Literature of Birmingham") and [culinary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_drink_in_Birmingham "Food and drink in Birmingham") scenes.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-27) Birmingham was the host city for the [2022 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Commonwealth_Games "2022 Commonwealth Games").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-CommonwealthSuccess-29) In 2021, Birmingham was the third most visited city in the UK by people from foreign nations.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-30)

## Toponymy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Toponymy")]

The name _Birmingham_ comes from the [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English "Old English")_Beormingahām_,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-31) meaning the "_[Beormingas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beormingas "Beormingas")_' home[land]" or "Beorma's people's home[land]/settlement" – _Beorminga_ was an [Anglo-Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon "Anglo-Saxon")[tribe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribe "Tribe") or [clan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan "Clan") whose name means 'Beorma's people' and which may have formed an early unit of [Anglo-Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon "Anglo-Saxon") administration. "_Beorma_" may be the name of the tribe leader. They are thought to have settled in modern-day [Digbeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digbeth "Digbeth"), [Central Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Birmingham "Central Birmingham"), on the banks of the [River Rea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Rea "River Rea").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-32)[Beorma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beorma "Beorma"), after whom the tribe was named, could have been its leader at the time of the Anglo-Saxon settlement, a shared ancestor, or a mythical tribal figurehead. Place names ending in _-ingahām_ are characteristic of primary settlements established during the early phases of Anglo-Saxon colonisation of an area, suggesting that Birmingham was probably in existence by the early 7th century at the latest.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-33) Surrounding settlements with names ending in _-tūn_ ('farm'), _-lēah_ ('woodland clearing'), _-worð_ ('enclosure') and _-field_ ('open ground') are likely to be secondary settlements created by the later expansion of the Anglo-Saxon population,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-34) in some cases possibly on earlier [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britons_(historical) "Britons (historical)") sites.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-35)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

Main articles: [History of Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Birmingham "History of Birmingham"), [Economic history of Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_history_of_Birmingham "Economic history of Birmingham"), [Science and invention in Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_and_invention_in_Birmingham "Science and invention in Birmingham"), and [Timeline of Birmingham history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Birmingham_history "Timeline of Birmingham history")

### Pre-history and medieval

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Pre-history and medieval")]

There is evidence of [early human](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_human "Early human") activity in the Birmingham area dating back to around 8000 BC,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-36) with [Stone Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_Age "Stone Age") artefacts suggesting seasonal settlements, overnight hunting parties and woodland activities such as tree felling.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-37) The many [burnt mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnt_mound "Burnt mound") that can still be seen around the city indicate that [modern humans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatomically_modern_humans "Anatomically modern humans") first intensively settled and cultivated the area during the [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age"), when a substantial but short-lived influx of population occurred between 1700 BC and 1000 BC, possibly caused by conflict or immigration in the surrounding area.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-38) During the 1st-century [Roman conquest of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_conquest_of_Britain "Roman conquest of Britain"), the forested country of the Birmingham Plateau formed a barrier to the advancing Roman legions,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-39) who built the large [Metchley Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metchley_Fort "Metchley Fort") in the area of modern-day [Edgbaston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgbaston "Edgbaston") in AD 48,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-40) and made it the focus of a network of [Roman roads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_roads_in_Britain "Roman roads in Britain").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-41) Birmingham was then later established by the _Beormingas_ around the 6th or 7th century as a small settlement in the then heavily forested [Arden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arden,_Warwickshire "Arden, Warwickshire") region in [Mercia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercia "Mercia").

The development of Birmingham into a significant urban and commercial centre began in 1166, when the [Lord of the manor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_of_the_manor "Lord of the manor") Peter de Bermingham obtained a charter to hold a market at [his castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Manor_House "Birmingham Manor House"), and followed this with the creation of a planned [market town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_town "Market town") and [seigneurial borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seigneurial_borough "Seigneurial borough") within his _[demesne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demesne "Demesne")_ or manorial estate, around the site that became the [Bull Ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bull_Ring,_Birmingham "Bull Ring, Birmingham").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-42) This established Birmingham as the primary commercial centre for the Birmingham Plateau at a time when the area's economy was expanding rapidly, with population growth nationally leading to the clearance, cultivation and settlement of previously marginal land.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-43) Within a century of the charter Birmingham had grown into a prosperous urban centre of merchants and craftsmen.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-44) By 1327 it was the third-largest town in Warwickshire,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Leather_2001_12-45) a position it would retain for the next 200 years.

### Early modern

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early modern")]

The principal governing institutions of medieval Birmingham – including the [Guild of the Holy Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guild_of_the_Holy_Cross_(Birmingham) "Guild of the Holy Cross (Birmingham)") and the lordship of the [de Birmingham family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Birmingham_family "De Birmingham family") – collapsed between 1536 and 1547,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-46) leaving the town with an unusually high degree of social and economic freedom and initiating a period of transition and growth.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-47)

The importance of the manufacture of [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") goods to Birmingham's economy was recognised as early as 1538, and grew rapidly as the century progressed.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-48) Equally significant was the town's emerging role as a centre for the [iron merchants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironmongers "Ironmongers") who organised finance, supplied raw materials and traded and marketed the industry's products.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-49) By the 1600s Birmingham formed the commercial hub of a network of [forges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forge "Forge") and [furnaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_furnace "Industrial furnace") stretching from [South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Wales "South Wales") to [Cheshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire "Cheshire")[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-50) and its merchants were selling finished manufactured goods as far afield as the [West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indies "West Indies").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-51) These trading links gave Birmingham's metalworkers access to much wider markets, allowing them to diversify away from lower-skilled trades producing basic goods for local sale, towards a broader range of specialist, higher-skilled and more lucrative activities.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-52)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Westley---East-Prospect-of-Birmingham-1732.jpg/250px-Westley---East-Prospect-of-Birmingham-1732.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Westley---East-Prospect-of-Birmingham-1732.jpg)

_The East Prospect of Birmingham_ (1732), engraving by William Westley

By the time of the [English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War") Birmingham's booming economy, its expanding population, and its resulting high levels of [social mobility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_mobility "Social mobility") and [cultural pluralism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_pluralism "Cultural pluralism"), had seen it develop new social structures very different from those of more established areas.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Hughes-p9-53) Relationships were built around pragmatic commercial linkages rather than the rigid paternalism and deference of [feudal society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_society "Feudal society"), and loyalties to the traditional hierarchies of the [established church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") and [aristocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_nobility "British nobility") were weak.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Hughes-p9-53) The town's reputation for [political radicalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_radicalism "Political radicalism") and its strongly [Parliamentarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") sympathies saw it attacked by [Royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalier "Cavalier") forces in the [Battle of Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Birmingham "Battle of Birmingham") in 1643,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-54) and it developed into a centre of [Puritanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puritanism "Puritanism") in the 1630s[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Hughes-p9-53) and as a haven for [Nonconformists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") from the 1660s.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-55)

By 1700 Birmingham's population had increased fifteen-fold and the town was the fifth-largest in England and Wales.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Berg_1991_180-56) The 18th century saw this tradition of free-thinking and collaboration blossom into the cultural phenomenon now known as the [Midlands Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midlands_Enlightenment "Midlands Enlightenment").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-57) The town developed into a notable centre of [literary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literature_of_Birmingham "Literature of Birmingham"), [musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music_of_Birmingham "Classical music of Birmingham"), [artistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_Birmingham "Art of Birmingham") and [theatrical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_of_Birmingham "Theatre of Birmingham") activity;[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-58) and its leading citizens – particularly the members of the [Lunar Society of Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Society_of_Birmingham "Lunar Society of Birmingham") – became influential participants in the circulation of [philosophical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophical "Philosophical") and [scientific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific "Scientific") ideas among Europe's intellectual elite.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-59) The close relationship between Enlightenment Birmingham's leading thinkers and its major manufacturers[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-60) – in men like [Matthew Boulton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Boulton "Matthew Boulton") and [James Keir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Keir "James Keir") they were often in fact the same people[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-61) – made it particularly important for the exchange of knowledge between pure science and the practical world of manufacturing and technology.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-62) This created a "chain reaction of innovation",[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-63) forming a pivotal link between the earlier [Scientific Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Revolution "Scientific Revolution") and the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution") that would follow.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-64)

### Industrial Revolution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Industrial Revolution")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Matthew_Boulton_-_Carl_Frederik_von_Breda.jpg/250px-Matthew_Boulton_-_Carl_Frederik_von_Breda.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Matthew_Boulton_-_Carl_Frederik_von_Breda.jpg)

[Matthew Boulton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Boulton "Matthew Boulton"), a prominent early industrialist

Birmingham's explosive industrial expansion started earlier than that of the [textile-manufacturing towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mill_town "Mill town") of the [North of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_of_England "North of England"),[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-65) and was driven by different factors. Instead of the [economies of scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economies_of_scale "Economies of scale") of a low-paid, unskilled workforce producing a single bulk [product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_(business) "Product (business)") such as cotton or wool in large, mechanised units of production, Birmingham's industrial development was built on the adaptability and creativity of a highly paid workforce with a strong [division of labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_labour "Division of labour"), practising a broad variety of skilled specialist trades and producing a constantly diversifying range of products, in a highly [entrepreneurial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entrepreneurial "Entrepreneurial") economy of small, often self-owned workshops.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-66) This led to exceptional levels of inventiveness: between 1760 and 1850 – the core years of the Industrial Revolution – Birmingham residents registered over three times as many [patents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent "Patent") as those of any other British town or city.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-67)

The demand for [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_(economics) "Capital (economics)") to feed rapid economic expansion also saw Birmingham grow into a major financial and commercial centre with extensive international connections.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Berg_1991_183-68)[Lloyds Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyds_Bank "Lloyds Bank") was founded in the town in 1765,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-69) and [Ketley's Building Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketley's_Building_Society "Ketley's Building Society"), the world's first [building society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_society "Building society"), in 1775.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-70) By 1800 the West Midlands had more banking offices per head than any other region in Britain, including London.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Berg_1991_183-68)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Soho_Manufactory_ca_1800.jpg/250px-Soho_Manufactory_ca_1800.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Soho_Manufactory_ca_1800.jpg)

The [Soho Manufactory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soho_Manufactory "Soho Manufactory") of 1765 – pioneer of the [factory system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factory_system "Factory system") and the [industrial steam engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt_steam_engine "Watt steam engine")

Innovation in 18th-century Birmingham often took the form of incremental series of small-scale improvements to existing products or processes,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-71) but also included major developments that lay at the heart of the emergence of [industrial society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_society "Industrial society").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-indsoc-18) In 1709 the Birmingham-trained [Abraham Darby I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Darby_I "Abraham Darby I") moved to [Coalbrookdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalbrookdale "Coalbrookdale") in [Shropshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shropshire "Shropshire") and built the first [blast furnace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blast_furnace "Blast furnace") to successfully smelt iron ore with [coke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coke_(fuel) "Coke (fuel)"), transforming the quality, volume and scale on which it was possible to produce [cast iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cast_iron "Cast iron").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-72) In 1732 [Lewis Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Paul "Lewis Paul") and [John Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wyatt_(inventor) "John Wyatt (inventor)") invented [roller spinning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roller_spinning "Roller spinning"), the "one novel idea of the first importance" in the development of the [mechanised cotton industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textile_manufacture_during_the_Industrial_Revolution "Textile manufacture during the Industrial Revolution").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-73) In 1741 they opened the [world's first cotton mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Priory_Cotton_Mill "Upper Priory Cotton Mill") in Birmingham's Upper Priory.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-74) In 1746 [John Roebuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Roebuck "John Roebuck") invented the [lead chamber process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_chamber_process "Lead chamber process"), enabling the large-scale manufacture of [sulphuric acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulphuric_acid "Sulphuric acid"),[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Hopkins_1989_20-75) and in 1780 James Keir developed a process for the bulk manufacture of [alkali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_carbonate "Sodium carbonate"),[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-76) together marking the birth of the modern [chemical industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_industry "Chemical industry").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-77) In 1765 [Matthew Boulton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Boulton "Matthew Boulton") opened the [Soho Manufactory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soho_Manufactory "Soho Manufactory"), pioneering the combination and mechanisation under one roof of previously separate manufacturing activities through a system known as "rational manufacture".[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-78) As the largest manufacturing unit in Europe, this came to symbolise the emergence of the [factory system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factory_system "Factory system").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-79)

Most significant, however, was the development in 1776 of the [industrial steam engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt_steam_engine "Watt steam engine") by [James Watt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watt "James Watt") and Matthew Boulton.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-80) Freeing for the first time the manufacturing capacity of human society from the limited availability of hand, water and animal power, this was arguably the pivotal moment of the entire [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution") and a key factor in the worldwide increases in productivity over the following century.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-81)

### Regency and Victorian

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Regency and Victorian")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Benjamin_Haydon_-_Meeting_of_the_Birmingham_Political_Union.jpg/250px-Benjamin_Haydon_-_Meeting_of_the_Birmingham_Political_Union.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Benjamin_Haydon_-_Meeting_of_the_Birmingham_Political_Union.jpg)

[Thomas Attwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Attwood_(economist) "Thomas Attwood (economist)") addressing a 200,000-strong meeting of the [Birmingham Political Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Political_Union "Birmingham Political Union") during the Days of May 1832 – oil on canvas by [Benjamin Haydon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Haydon "Benjamin Haydon") (c.1832–1833)

Birmingham rose to national political prominence in the campaign for political reform in the early 19th century, with [Thomas Attwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Attwood_(economist) "Thomas Attwood (economist)") and the [Birmingham Political Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Political_Union "Birmingham Political Union") bringing the country to the brink of civil war during the [Days of May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Days_of_May "Days of May") that preceded the passing of the [Reform Act 1832](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Act_1832 "Reform Act 1832").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-82) The union's meetings on [Newhall Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newhall_Street "Newhall Street") in 1831 and 1832 were the largest political assemblies Britain had ever seen.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-83)[Lord Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lambton,_1st_Earl_of_Durham "John Lambton, 1st Earl of Durham"), who drafted the act, wrote that "the country owed Reform to Birmingham, and its salvation from revolution".[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-84) This reputation for having "shaken the fabric of privilege to its base" in 1832 led [John Bright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bright "John Bright") to make Birmingham the platform for his successful campaign for the [Reform Act 1867](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Act_1867 "Reform Act 1867"), which extended voting rights to the urban working class.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-85)

The original [charter of incorporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_of_incorporation "Charter of incorporation"), dated 31 October 1838, was received in Birmingham on 1 November, then read in the [town hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Town_Hall "Birmingham Town Hall") on 5 November with elections for the first [Birmingham Town Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Town_Council "Birmingham Town Council") being held on 26 December. Sixteen aldermen and 48 councillors were elected and the borough was divided into 13 wards. [William Scholefield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Scholefield "William Scholefield") became the first mayor and William Redfern was appointed as town clerk. [Birmingham Town Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Town_Police "Birmingham Town Police") were established the following year.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Birmingham's tradition of innovation continued into the 19th century. By the 1820s, [the country's extensive canal system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canals_of_the_United_Kingdom "Canals of the United Kingdom") had been constructed, giving greater access to natural resources and fuel for industries. Birmingham was the terminus for both of the world's first two long-distance railway lines: the 82-mile (132 km)[Grand Junction Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Junction_Railway "Grand Junction Railway") of 1837 and the 112-mile (180 km)[London and Birmingham Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_Birmingham_Railway "London and Birmingham Railway") of 1838.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-86) Birmingham schoolteacher [Rowland Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowland_Hill "Rowland Hill") invented the [postage stamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postage_stamp "Postage stamp") and created the first modern universal [postal system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_system "Postal system") in 1839.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-87)[Alexander Parkes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Parkes "Alexander Parkes") invented the first human-made [plastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic "Plastic") in the [Jewellery Quarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewellery_Quarter "Jewellery Quarter") in 1855.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-88)

During the [Victorian era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era "Victorian era"), the population of Birmingham grew rapidly to well over half a million[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-historicpopulation-89) and Birmingham became the second largest population centre in England. Birmingham was granted [city status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_status_in_the_United_Kingdom "City status in the United Kingdom") in 1889 by [Queen Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria "Queen Victoria").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-90)[Joseph Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Chamberlain "Joseph Chamberlain"), mayor of Birmingham and later an MP, and his son [Neville Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Chamberlain "Neville Chamberlain"), who was Lord Mayor of Birmingham and later the British Prime Minister, are two of the most well-known political figures who have lived in Birmingham. The city established [its own university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham "University of Birmingham") in 1900.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-91)

### 20th century and contemporary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 20th century and contemporary")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Bull_Ring_Blitz.jpg/250px-Bull_Ring_Blitz.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bull_Ring_Blitz.jpg)

Ruins of the [Bull Ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bull_Ring,_Birmingham "Bull Ring, Birmingham"), destroyed during the [Birmingham Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Blitz "Birmingham Blitz"), 1940

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Birmingham%2C_England%2C_1946.png/250px-Birmingham%2C_England%2C_1946.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Birmingham,_England,_1946.png)

An aerial photograph of Birmingham in 1946

The city suffered heavy bomb damage during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II")'s "[Birmingham Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Blitz "Birmingham Blitz")". The city was also the scene of two scientific discoveries that were to prove critical to the outcome of the war.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-92)[Otto Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Frisch "Otto Frisch") and [Rudolf Peierls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Peierls "Rudolf Peierls") first described how a practical [nuclear weapon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") could be constructed in the [Frisch–Peierls memorandum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisch%E2%80%93Peierls_memorandum "Frisch–Peierls memorandum") of 1940,[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-93) the same year that the [cavity magnetron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavity_magnetron "Cavity magnetron"), the key component of [radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar "Radar") and later of [microwave ovens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microwave_oven "Microwave oven"), was invented by [John Randall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Randall_(physicist) "John Randall (physicist)") and [Harry Boot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Boot "Harry Boot").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-94) Details of these two discoveries, together with an outline of the first [jet engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_engine "Jet engine") invented by [Frank Whittle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Whittle "Frank Whittle") in nearby [Rugby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby,_Warwickshire "Rugby, Warwickshire"), were taken to the United States by the [Tizard Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tizard_Mission "Tizard Mission") in September 1940, in a single black box later described by an official American historian as "the most valuable cargo ever brought to our shores".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-95)

The city was extensively redeveloped during the 1950s and 1960s.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-97) This included the construction of large [tower block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_block "Tower block") estates, such as [Castle Vale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Vale "Castle Vale"). The [Bull Ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bull_Ring,_Birmingham "Bull Ring, Birmingham") was reconstructed and [New Street station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Street_station "New Street station") was redeveloped. In the decades following World War II, the ethnic makeup of Birmingham changed significantly, as it received waves of immigration from the [Commonwealth of Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") and beyond.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-98) The city's population peaked in 1951 at 1,113,000 residents.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-historicpopulation-89)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/5c/Mulberry_bush_pub_bomb.jpg/250px-Mulberry_bush_pub_bomb.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mulberry_bush_pub_bomb.jpg)

Aftermath of the bomb attack on the Mulberry Bush Pub during the [pub bombings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_pub_bombings "Birmingham pub bombings") of 1974

21 people were killed and 182 were injured in [a series of bomb attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_pub_bombings "Birmingham pub bombings") in 1974, thought to be carried out by the [Provisional IRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_IRA "Provisional IRA"). The bombings were the worst terror attacks in England up until the [2005 London bombings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_London_bombings "2005 London bombings")[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-99) and consisted of bombs being planted in two [pubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pubs "Pubs") in central Birmingham. Six men were convicted, who became known later as the [Birmingham Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Six "Birmingham Six") and sentenced to life imprisonment. They were acquitted after 16 years by the [Court of Appeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Appeal_(England_and_Wales) "Court of Appeal (England and Wales)").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-100) The convictions are now considered one of the worst miscarriages of justice in the UK in recent times. The true perpetrators of the attacks are yet to be arrested.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Birmingham_Bombings_1976-101)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-102)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-103)

Birmingham remained by far Britain's most prosperous provincial city as late as the 1970s,[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-104) with household incomes exceeding even those of London and the [South East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_East_England "South East England"),[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-105) but its economic diversity and capacity for regeneration declined in the decades that followed World War II as [Central Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom") sought to restrict the city's growth and disperse industry and population to the stagnating areas of Wales and [Northern England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_England "Northern England").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-106) These measures hindered "the natural self-regeneration of businesses in Birmingham, leaving it top-heavy with the old and infirm",[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-107) and the city became increasingly dependent on the [motor industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_industry_in_the_United_Kingdom "Automotive industry in the United Kingdom"). The [recession of the early 1980s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_1980s_recession "Early 1980s recession") saw Birmingham's economy collapse, with unprecedented levels of unemployment and [outbreaks of social unrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Handsworth_riots "1985 Handsworth riots") in inner-city districts.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-108)

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Birmingham_2022_Opening_Ceremony.jpg/250px-Birmingham_2022_Opening_Ceremony.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Birmingham_2022_Opening_Ceremony.jpg)

The opening ceremony of the [2022 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Commonwealth_Games "2022 Commonwealth Games") in Birmingham

Since the turn of the 21st century, many parts of Birmingham have been transformed, with the redevelopment of the [Bullring Shopping Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullring_Shopping_Centre "Bullring Shopping Centre"),[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-109) the construction of the new Library of Birmingham (the largest public library in Europe) and the completed regeneration of old industrial areas such as [Brindleyplace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brindleyplace "Brindleyplace"), [The Mailbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mailbox "The Mailbox") and the [International Convention Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Convention_Centre,_Birmingham "International Convention Centre, Birmingham"), ongoing rebuilding of [Eastside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastside,_Birmingham "Eastside, Birmingham"), [Digbeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digbeth "Digbeth"), and [Centenary Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centenary_Square "Centenary Square"), as well as the rationalisation of the [Inner Ring Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensway,_Birmingham "Queensway, Birmingham"). In 1998 Birmingham hosted the [24th G8 summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24th_G8_summit "24th G8 summit"). The city successfully hosted the [2022 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Commonwealth_Games "2022 Commonwealth Games").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-110)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-CommonwealthSuccess-29)

## Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Governance")]

Main article: [Government of Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Birmingham "Government of Birmingham")

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Birmingham_City_Hall.jpg/250px-Birmingham_City_Hall.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Birmingham_City_Hall.jpg)

The [Council House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_House,_Birmingham "Council House, Birmingham"), headquarters of [Birmingham City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_City_Council "Birmingham City Council")

[Birmingham City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_City_Council "Birmingham City Council") has 104 [councillors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Councillor "Councillor") representing 69 [wards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ward_(politics) "Ward (politics)") as of 2026.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-111) Its headquarters are at the [Council House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_House,_Birmingham "Council House, Birmingham") in [Victoria Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Square,_Birmingham "Victoria Square, Birmingham"). As of 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit), the council has no overall majority. A group of [Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_England_and_Wales "Green Party of England and Wales"), [Lib Dem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)") and [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_politician "Independent politician") councillors form an administration, which is led by Lib Dem councillor Roger Harmer.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-112)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-113) Labour held a majority from the May 2012 elections to May 2026.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-114) The honour and dignity of a [Lord Mayoralty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mayors_of_Birmingham "Lord Mayors of Birmingham") was conferred on Birmingham by [Letters Patent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letters_Patent "Letters Patent") on 3 June 1896.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-115)

Birmingham's ten [parliamentary constituencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituencies_of_the_Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom "Constituencies of the Parliament of the United Kingdom") are represented in the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom")as of 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit) by one [Conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)"), one independent and eight [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)")[MPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-116)

Originally part of [Warwickshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwickshire "Warwickshire"), Birmingham expanded in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, absorbing parts of [Worcestershire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcestershire "Worcestershire") to the south and [Staffordshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staffordshire "Staffordshire") to the north and west. The city absorbed [Sutton Coldfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_Coldfield "Sutton Coldfield") in 1974 and became a metropolitan borough in the new [West Midlands county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_county "West Midlands county"),[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-lga1972-117) comprising Birmingham, [Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_City_Council "Coventry City Council"), [Dudley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dudley_Metropolitan_Borough_Council "Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council"), [Sandwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandwell_Metropolitan_Borough_Council "Sandwell Metropolitan Borough Council"), [Solihull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solihull_Metropolitan_Borough_Council "Solihull Metropolitan Borough Council"), [Walsall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walsall_Council "Walsall Council"), and [Wolverhampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Wolverhampton_Council "City of Wolverhampton Council"). A top-level government body, the [West Midlands Combined Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_Combined_Authority "West Midlands Combined Authority"), was formed in April 2016. The WMCA holds devolved powers in transport, development planning, economic growth, and large-scale investment. The authority is governed by a [directly elected mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_West_Midlands "Mayor of West Midlands"), currently Labour's [Richard Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Parker_(mayor) "Richard Parker (mayor)"), similar to the [Mayor of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_London "Mayor of London").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-118)

On 5 September 2023, Birmingham city council issued a Section 114 notice to say that it could not meet its financial commitments after an equal pay lawsuit.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-119) Effectively this meant the council was bankrupt. Major contributing factors include a £1.1 billion sum that has been paid out since 2010 for equal pay claims, an ongoing bill for £760 million, increasing by £14 million a month, and problems with a new IT system that was projected to cost £19 million, but is now closer to £100 million. There is a projected £87 million deficit for the financial year 2023/2024.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-120)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Geography")]

Further information: [List of areas of Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_areas_of_Birmingham "List of areas of Birmingham")

Birmingham is located in the centre of the [West Midlands region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_region "West Midlands region") of England on the [Birmingham Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Plateau "Birmingham Plateau") – an area of relatively high ground, ranging between 500 and 1,000 feet (150 and 300 metres)[above sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_sea_level "Above sea level") and crossed by Britain's main north–south [watershed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_divide "Water divide") between the basins of the Rivers [Severn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severn "Severn") and [Trent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Trent "River Trent"). To the immediate south west of the city lie the [Lickey Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lickey_Hills "Lickey Hills"),[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-121)[Clent Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clent_Hills "Clent Hills") and [Walton Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walton_Hill "Walton Hill"), which reach 1,033 feet (315 m) and have extensive views over the city. Birmingham is drained only by minor rivers and brooks, primarily the [River Tame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tame,_West_Midlands "River Tame, West Midlands") and its tributaries the [Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Cole,_West_Midlands "River Cole, West Midlands") and the [Rea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Rea "River Rea"). Birmingham is located significantly inland, and its nearest body of sea is at [Liverpool Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Bay "Liverpool Bay"). It lies at the same latitude as [Lowestoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowestoft "Lowestoft"), Britain's easternmost settlement; it is therefore much more proximate to the western coast of Wales, at [Cardigan Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardigan_Bay "Cardigan Bay").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-122)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-123)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Octagon_Skyline.png/250px-Octagon_Skyline.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Octagon_Skyline.png)

The cityscape of Birmingham

The City of Birmingham forms a [conurbation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conurbation "Conurbation") with the borough of [Solihull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Borough_of_Solihull "Metropolitan Borough of Solihull") to the south east, and with the city of [Wolverhampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolverhampton "Wolverhampton") and the industrial towns of the [Black Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Country "Black Country") to the north west, which form the [West Midlands Built-up Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_Built-up_Area "West Midlands Built-up Area") covering 59,972 ha (600 km 2; 232 sq mi).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Surrounding this is [Birmingham's metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_metropolitan_area "Birmingham metropolitan area") – the area to which it is closely economically tied through [commuting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuting "Commuting") – which includes the towns of [Tamworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamworth,_Staffordshire "Tamworth, Staffordshire") and [Cannock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannock "Cannock") to the north; the city of [Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry "Coventry") and the towns of [Nuneaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuneaton "Nuneaton"), [Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick "Warwick") and [Leamington Spa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leamington_Spa "Leamington Spa") to the east in Warwickshire and the Worcestershire towns of [Redditch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redditch "Redditch"), [Kidderminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidderminster "Kidderminster") and [Bromsgrove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromsgrove "Bromsgrove") to the south west.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-espon-124)

As the crow flies, Birmingham lies approximately 100 miles (160 km) north-west of [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), 85 miles (137 km) north-east of the Welsh capital [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff "Cardiff"), 45 miles (72 km) south-west of [Nottingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nottingham "Nottingham"), 70 miles (110 km) south of [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester"), and 75 miles (121 km) north-north-east of [Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol "Bristol").

Much of the area now occupied by the city was originally a northern reach of the ancient [Forest of Arden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_of_Arden "Forest of Arden") and the city remains relatively densely covered by [oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak "Oak") in a large number of districts such as [Moseley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moseley "Moseley"), [Saltley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltley "Saltley"), [Yardley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yardley,_Birmingham "Yardley, Birmingham"), [Stirchley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirchley,_West_Midlands "Stirchley, West Midlands") and [Hockley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hockley,_Birmingham "Hockley, Birmingham"). These places, with names ending in "-ley", deriving from [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English "Old English")_-\_lēah\__ meaning "woodland clearing", are named after the former forest.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-125)

### Geology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Geology")]

Birmingham is dominated by the Birmingham Fault, which runs diagonally through the city from the Lickey Hills in the south west, passing through Edgbaston and the Bull Ring, to [Erdington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erdington "Erdington") and Sutton Coldfield in the north east.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-JPS-126) To the south and east of the fault the ground is largely softer [Mercia Mudstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercia_Mudstone "Mercia Mudstone"), interspersed with beds of [Bunter pebbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunter_(geology) "Bunter (geology)") and crossed by the valleys of the Rivers Tame, Rea and Cole and their tributaries.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-127) To the north and west of the fault, between 150 and 600 feet (46 and 183 metres) higher than the surrounding area and underlying much of the city centre, lies a long ridge of harder [Keuper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keuper "Keuper")[Sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone").[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-128)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-129) The bedrock underlying Birmingham was mostly laid down during the [Permian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian "Permian") and [Triassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triassic "Triassic") periods.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-JPS-126)

The area has evidence of [glacial deposits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_deposit "Glacial deposit"), with prominent [erratic boulders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erratic_boulder "Erratic boulder") becoming a tourist attraction in the early 1900s.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-130)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-131)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-132)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Climate")]

Birmingham has a [temperate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate "Temperate")[maritime climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_climate "Maritime climate") (_Cfb_ according to the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification")), like much of the British Isles, with average maximum temperatures in summer (July) being about 21.3°C (70.3°F); and in winter (January) about 6.7°C (44.1°F).[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-133) Between 1971 and 2000 the warmest day of the year on average was 28.8°C (83.8°F)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-134) and the coldest night typically fell to −9.0°C (15.8°F).[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-135) Some 11.2 days each year rose to a temperature of 25.1°C (77.2°F) or above[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-136) and 51.6 nights reported an air frost.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-137) The highest recorded temperature recorded at the [Edgbaston Campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#Edgbaston_campus "University of Birmingham") was 37.4°C (99.3°F),[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-138) whilst a temperature of 37.0°C (98.6°F) was recorded at Birmingham Airport on the city's eastern edge, both recorded on [19 July 2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_European_heatwaves "2022 European heatwaves").[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-139)

Like most other large cities, Birmingham has a considerable [urban heat island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_heat_island "Urban heat island") effect.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-140) During the coldest night recorded, 14 January 1982, the temperature fell to −20.8°C (−5.4°F) at Birmingham Airport, but just −14.3°C (6.3°F) at Edgbaston, near the city centre.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-141) Birmingham is a snowy city relative to other large UK conurbations, due to its inland location and comparatively high elevation.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-RCBI-142) Between 1961 and 1990 [Birmingham Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Airport "Birmingham Airport") averaged 13.0 days of snow lying annually,[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-143) compared to 5.33 at [London Heathrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport "Heathrow Airport").[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-144) Snow showers often pass through the city via the [Cheshire gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire_gap "Cheshire gap") on north westerly airstreams, but can also come off the [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea") from north easterly airstreams.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-RCBI-142)

The city has been known to experience [tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado"): according to TORRO, Birmingham experienced 15 significant tornadoes between 1946 and 2005, with some being incredibly destructive. Most notably, a [deadly F3 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1931_Birmingham_tornado "1931 Birmingham tornado") on June 14, 1931, and another [IF3 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Birmingham_tornado "2005 Birmingham tornado") which followed a similar path on 28 July 2005, becoming the United Kingdom's costliest tornado on record.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-:0-145)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-146) On 23 November 1981, during a record-breaking [nationwide tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1981_United_Kingdom_tornado_outbreak "1981 United Kingdom tornado outbreak"), three tornadoes touched down within the Birmingham city limits – in Erdington, [Selly Oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selly_Oak "Selly Oak"), and King's Heath–with three more tornadoes touching down within the boundaries of the wider [West Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_(county) "West Midlands (county)") county.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-147)[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-:0-145) Notable tornadoes also struck the city in 1946, 1968, and 1999.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-:0-145)

### Environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Birmingham&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Environment")]

Further information: [Parks and open spaces in Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parks_and_open_spaces_in_Birmingham "Parks and open spaces in Birmingham") and [West Midlands Green Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_Green_Belt "West Midlands Green Belt")

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Birmingham_Botanical_Gardens._-_geograph.org.uk_-_835643.jpg/250px-Birmingham_Botanical_Gardens._-_geograph.org.uk_-_835643.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Birmingham_Botanical_Gardens._-_geograph.org.uk_-_835643.jpg)

[Birmingham Botanical Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Botanical_Gardens_(United_Kingdom) "Birmingham Botanical Gardens (United Kingdom)")

There are 571 parks within Birmingham[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Biophilic-159) – more than any other European city[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-QuickandQuirkyFacts2-160) – totalling over 3,500 hectares (14 sq mi) of public open space.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Biophilic-159) The city has over six million trees,[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-QuickandQuirkyFacts2-160) and 250 miles (400 kilometres) of urban brooks and streams.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Biophilic-159)[Sutton Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_Park,_West_Midlands "Sutton Park, West Midlands"), which covers 2,400 acres (971 ha) in the north of the city,[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-161) is the largest urban park in Europe and a [national nature reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_nature_reserves_in_England "National nature reserves in England").[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-Biophilic-159)[Birmingham Botanical Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Botanical_Gardens_(United_Kingdom) "Birmingham Botanical Gardens (United Kingdom)"), located close to the city centre, retains the [regency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regency_era "Regency era") landscape of its original design by [J. C. Loudon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._C._Loudon "J. C. Loudon") in 1829,[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-162) while the [Winterbourne Botanic Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winterbourne_Botanic_Garden "Winterbourne Botanic Garden") in [Edgbaston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgbaston "Edgbaston") reflects the more informal [Arts and Crafts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_and_Crafts "Arts and Crafts") tastes of its [Edwardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwardian "Edwardian") origins.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham#cite_note-163)

Several green spaces within the borough are designated as [green belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_belt_(United_Kingdom) "Green belt (United Kingdom)"), as a portion of the wider West Midlands Green Belt. This is a strategic local government policy used to prevent [urban sprawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_sprawl "Urban sprawl") and preserve [greenfield land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenfield_land "Greenfield land"). Areas included are the aforementioned Sutton Park; land along the borough boundary by the Sutton Coldfield, Walmley and Minworth suburbs; Kingfisher, Sheldon, Woodgate Valley country parks; grounds by the Wake Green football club; Bartley and Frankley reservoirs; and Handsworth cemetery with surrounding golf courses
