It was largely owing to Chamberlain's enthusiasm that the university was granted a [royal charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") by [Queen Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_of_the_United_Kingdom "Victoria of the United Kingdom") on 24 March 1900.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-18) The [Calthorpe family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gough-Calthorpe_family "Gough-Calthorpe family") offered twenty-five acres (10 hectares) of land on the [Bournbrook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bournbrook "Bournbrook") side of their estate in July. The Court of Governors received the **Birmingham University Act 1900** ([63 & 64 Vict.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/63_&_64_Vict. "63 & 64 Vict.") c. xix), which put the royal charter into effect on 31 May.

The transfer of Mason University College to the new University of Birmingham, with Chamberlain as its first [chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education) "Chancellor (education)") and Sir [Oliver Lodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Lodge "Oliver Lodge") as the first [principal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_(university) "Principal (university)"), was complete. A remnant of Josiah Mason's legacy is the Mermaid from his coat-of-arms, which appears in the sinister chief of the university shield and of his college, the double-headed lion in the dexter.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-19)

The commerce faculty was founded by Sir [William Ashley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Ashley_(economic_historian) "William Ashley (economic historian)") in 1901, who from 1902 until 1923 served as first Professor of Commerce and Dean of the Faculty. From 1905 to 1908, [Edward Elgar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Elgar "Edward Elgar") held the position of Peyton Professor of Music at the university. He was succeeded by his friend [Granville Bantock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granville_Bantock "Granville Bantock").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Anderton-20)

The university's own heritage archives are accessible for research through the university's Cadbury Research Library which is open to all interested researchers.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-21)

During the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), the Great Hall in the Aston Webb Building was requisitioned by the [War Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Office "War Office") to create the 1st Southern General Hospital, a facility for the [Royal Army Medical Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Army_Medical_Corps "Royal Army Medical Corps") to treat military casualties; it was equipped with 520 beds and treated 125,000 injured servicemen.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-birmingham.ac.uk-22)

In June 1921, the university appointed [Linetta de Castelvecchio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linetta_de_Castelvecchio "Linetta de Castelvecchio") as [Serena Professor of Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serena_Professor_of_Italian "Serena Professor of Italian"): she was the first woman to hold a chair at the university and one of the first women professors in Great Britain.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-24)

In 1939, the [Barber Institute of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barber_Institute_of_Fine_Arts "Barber Institute of Fine Arts"), designed by [Robert Atkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Atkinson_(architect) "Robert Atkinson (architect)"), was opened. In 1956, the first MSc programme in [Geotechnical Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geotechnical_Engineering "Geotechnical Engineering") commenced under the title of "Foundation Engineering", and has been run annually at the university since.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Sir Raymond Priestley, vice-chancellor in 1938, helped establish the first undergraduate courses in Physical Education in 1946, developed their sports facilities – starting with the gymnasium in 1939, and made participation in recreational sport compulsory for all new undergraduates from 1940 to 1968.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Birmingham became the first UK university to offer a sports degree.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The UK's longest-running MSc programme in Physics and Technology of Nuclear Reactors also started at the university in 1956, the same year that the world's first commercial nuclear power station was opened at [Calder Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calder_Hall "Calder Hall") in Cumbria.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1957, Sir [Hugh Casson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Casson "Hugh Casson") and Neville Conder were asked by the university to prepare a masterplan on the site of the original 1900 buildings, which were incomplete. The university drafted in other architects to amend the masterplan produced by the group. During the 1960s, the university constructed numerous large buildings, expanding the campus.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-hickman-25) In 1963, the university helped in the establishment of the faculty of medicine at the University of Rhodesia, now the [University of Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Zimbabwe "University of Zimbabwe") (UZ). UZ is now independent but both institutions maintain relations through student exchange programmes.

Birmingham also supported the creation of [Keele University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keele_University "Keele University") (formerly University College of North Staffordshire) and the [University of Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick "University of Warwick") under the Vice-Chancellorship of Sir Robert Aitken who acted as 'godfather' to the University of Warwick.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-26) The initial plan was to establish a satellite university college in [Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry "Coventry") but Aitken advised an independent initiative to the University Grants Committee.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-27)

[Malcolm X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_X "Malcolm X"), the Afro-American human rights activist, addressed the University Debating Society in 1965.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-birmingham.ac.uk-22)

### Scientific discoveries and inventions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Scientific discoveries and inventions")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Aston_Webb_Building_Entrance_Statues_University_of_Birmingham.JPG/250px-Aston_Webb_Building_Entrance_Statues_University_of_Birmingham.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aston_Webb_Building_Entrance_Statues_University_of_Birmingham.JPG)

Statues of the University of Birmingham (Beethoven, Virgil, Michelangelo, Plato, Shakespeare, Newton, Watt, Faraday, and Darwin)

The university has been involved in many scientific breakthroughs and inventions. From 1925 until 1948, Sir [Norman Haworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Haworth "Norman Haworth") was Professor and Director of the Department of Chemistry. He was appointed Dean of the Faculty of Science and acted as Vice-Principal from 1947 until 1948. His research focused predominantly on [carbohydrate chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate_chemistry "Carbohydrate chemistry") in which he confirmed a number of structures of optically active sugars. By 1928, he had deduced and confirmed the structures of [maltose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maltose "Maltose"), [cellobiose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellobiose "Cellobiose"), [lactose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lactose "Lactose"), [gentiobiose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentiobiose "Gentiobiose"), [melibiose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melibiose "Melibiose"), gentianose, [raffinose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raffinose "Raffinose"), as well as the [glucoside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucoside "Glucoside") ring tautomeric structure of aldose sugars. His research helped to define the basic features of the [starch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starch "Starch"), [cellulose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellulose "Cellulose"), [glycogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glycogen "Glycogen"), [inulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inulin "Inulin") and [xylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xylan "Xylan") molecules. He also contributed towards solving the problems with bacterial polysaccharides. He was a recipient of the [Nobel Prize in Chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry") in 1937.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-28)

The [cavity magnetron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavity_magnetron "Cavity magnetron") was developed in the Department of Physics by Sir [John Randall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Randall_(physicist) "John Randall (physicist)"), [Harry Boot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Boot "Harry Boot") and [James Sayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Sayers_(physicist) "James Sayers (physicist)"). This was vital to the Allied victory in World War II. In 1940, the [Frisch–Peierls memorandum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisch%E2%80%93Peierls_memorandum "Frisch–Peierls memorandum"), a document which demonstrated that the [atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb") was more than simply theoretically possible, was written in the Physics Department by Sir [Rudolf Peierls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Peierls "Rudolf Peierls") and [Otto Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Frisch "Otto Frisch"). The university also hosted early work on [gaseous diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaseous_diffusion "Gaseous diffusion") in the Chemistry department when it was located in the Hills building.

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Poynting_Physics_building_2.jpg/250px-Poynting_Physics_building_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Poynting_Physics_building_2.jpg)

Poynting Physics building

Physicist Sir [Mark Oliphant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Oliphant "Mark Oliphant") made a proposal for the construction of a proton-[synchrotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchrotron "Synchrotron") in 1943; however, he made no assertion that the machine would work. In 1945, phase stability was discovered; consequently, the proposal was revived, and construction of a machine that could surpass proton energies of 1[GeV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GeV "GeV") began at the university. However, because of lack of funds, the machine did not start until 1953. The [Brookhaven National Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookhaven_National_Laboratory "Brookhaven National Laboratory") managed to beat them; they started their [Cosmotron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmotron "Cosmotron") in 1952, and had it entirely working in 1953, before the University of Birmingham.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-29)

In 1947, Sir [Peter Medawar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Medawar "Peter Medawar") was appointed Mason Professor of Zoology at the university. His work involved investigating the phenomenon of tolerance and transplantation immunity. He collaborated with [Rupert E. Billingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupert_E._Billingham "Rupert E. Billingham") and they did research on problems of pigmentation and [skin grafting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skin_grafting "Skin grafting") in cattle. They used skin grafting to differentiate between monozygotic and dizygotic twins in cattle. Taking the earlier research of R. D. Owen into consideration, they concluded that actively acquired tolerance of homografts could be artificially reproduced. For this research, Medawar was elected a [Fellow of the Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow_of_the_Royal_Society "Fellow of the Royal Society"). He left Birmingham in 1951 and joined the faculty at [University College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_London "University College London"), where he continued his research on transplantation immunity. He was a recipient of the [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine "Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine") in 1960.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Medawar-30)

### Recent history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Recent history")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/The_new_school_of_Engineering_Building%2C_University_of_Birmingham.jpg/250px-The_new_school_of_Engineering_Building%2C_University_of_Birmingham.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_new_school_of_Engineering_Building,_University_of_Birmingham.jpg)

The construction of new school of Engineering was completed in 2021.

In 1999, talks commenced on the possibility of [Aston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_University "Aston University") integrating itself into the University of Birmingham as the University of Birmingham, Aston Campus. This would have resulted in the University of Birmingham expanding to become one of the largest universities in the UK, with a student body of 30,000. Talks were halted in 2001 after Aston University determined the timing to be inopportune. While Aston University management was in favour of the integration, and reception among staff was generally positive, the Aston student union voted two-to-one against the integration. Despite this set back, the Vice Chancellor of the University of Birmingham said the door remained open to recommence talks when Aston University is ready.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-31)

The [final round](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_general_election_debates,_2010#Prime_Ministerial_Debate:_economic_affairs "United Kingdom general election debates, 2010") of the first ever televised leaders' debates, hosted by the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"), was held at the university during the [2010 British general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_Kingdom_general_election "2010 United Kingdom general election") campaign on 29 April 2010.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-33)

On 9 August 2010 the university announced that for the first time it would not enter the [UCAS clearing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clearing_system "Clearing system") process for 2010 admission, which matches under-subscribed courses to students who did not meet their firm or insurance choices, owing to all places being taken. Largely a result of the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"), Birmingham joined fellow Russell Group universities including Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh and Bristol in not offering any clearing places.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-34)

The university acted as a training camp for the [Jamaican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica_at_the_Olympics "Jamaica at the Olympics") athletics team prior to the [2012 London Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_London_Olympics "2012 London Olympics").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Jamaica-35)

A new library was opened for the 2016/17 academic year, and a new sports centre opened in May 2017.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-36) The previous Main Library and the old Munrow Sports Centre, including the athletics track, have both since been demolished, with the demolition of the old library being completed in November 2017.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-37)

Birmingham was selected as the host for the [2022 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Commonwealth_Games "2022 Commonwealth Games") and was the venue for hockey and squash, owing to the ability of existing facilities to host the games. The university was the largest athletes village during the games, hosting 3,500 athletes in Tennis Courts and the Vale, and was the official training venue for both swimming and athletics.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-38)

### Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Controversies")]

Please help [integrate negative information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Structure "Wikipedia:Structure") into other sections or remove [undue focus on minor criticisms and controversies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:BALASP "Wikipedia:BALASP")._(May 2021)_

The discipline of [cultural studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_studies "Cultural studies") was founded at the university and between 1964 and 2002 the campus was home to the [Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Contemporary_Cultural_Studies "Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies"), a research centre whose members' work came to be known as the Birmingham School of Cultural Studies. Despite being established by one of the key figures in the field, [Richard Hoggart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Hoggart "Richard Hoggart"), and being later directed by the theorist [Stuart Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Hall_(cultural_theorist) "Stuart Hall (cultural theorist)"), the department was controversially closed down.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-39)

Analysis showed that the university was fourth in a list of British universities that faced the most [employment tribunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Employment_tribunal "Employment tribunal") claims between 2008 and 2011. They were the second most likely to settle these before the hearing date.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-40)

In 2011, a parliamentary [early day motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_day_motion "Early day motion") was proposed, arguing against the Guild suspending the elected Sabbatical Vice President (Education), who was arrested while taking part in protest activity.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-41)

In December 2011, it was announced that the university had obtained a 12-month-long injunction[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-42) against a group of around 25 students, who occupied a residential building on campus from 23 to 26 November 2011, preventing them from engaging in further "occupational protest action" on the university's grounds without prior permission. It was misreported in the press that this injunction applied to all students; the court order defines the defendants as,

> Persons unknown (including students of the University of Birmingham) entering or remaining upon the buildings known as No. 2 Lodge Pritchatts Road, Birmingham at the University of Birmingham for the purpose of protest action (without the consent of the University of Birmingham).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-43)

The university and the Guild of Students also clarified the scope of the injunction in an e-mail sent to all students on 11 January 2012, stating that "The injunction applies to only those individuals who occupied the lodge".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-44) The university said that it sought this injunction as a safety precaution based on a previous occupation.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-45) Three human rights groups, including [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International"), condemned the move as restrictive on human rights.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-46)

In 2019, several women said the university refused to investigate allegations of [campus rape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campus_rape "Campus rape"). One student who complained of rape in university accommodation was told by employees of the university that there were no specific procedures for handling rape complaints. In other cases students were told they would have to prove the alleged rapes occurred on university property. The university has been criticized by legal professionals for not adequately assessing the risk to students by refusing to investigate complaints of criminal conduct.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-47)

In June 2022, the University published a report into, and apologised for, its involvement in developing, promoting and administering electric-shock [conversion therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_therapy "Conversion therapy") to gay men, during the period 1966–1983.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-49)

### Edgbaston campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Edgbaston campus")]

#### Original buildings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Original buildings")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Plan_Edgbaston_University_1909.jpg/250px-Plan_Edgbaston_University_1909.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plan_Edgbaston_University_1909.jpg)

Plan of the new University Campus at [Edgbaston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgbaston "Edgbaston"), proposed by architects Sir Aston Webb and Mr Ingress Bell in 1909

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/BirminghamUniversityChancellorsCourt.jpg/250px-BirminghamUniversityChancellorsCourt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BirminghamUniversityChancellorsCourt.jpg)

The [Aston Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_Webb "Aston Webb") Buildings, Chancellor's Court

The main campus of the university occupies a site some 3 miles (4.8 km) south-west of [Birmingham city centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_city_centre "Birmingham city centre"), in [Edgbaston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgbaston "Edgbaston"). It is arranged around [Joseph Chamberlain Memorial Clock Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Chamberlain_Memorial_Clock_Tower "Joseph Chamberlain Memorial Clock Tower") (affectionately known as "Old Joe" or "Big Joe"), a grand [campanile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campanile "Campanile") which commemorates the university's first chancellor, [Joseph Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Chamberlain "Joseph Chamberlain").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-50) Chamberlain may be considered the founder of the University of Birmingham, and was largely responsible for the university gaining its Royal Charter in 1900 and for the development of the Edgbaston campus. The university's Great Hall is located in the domed [Aston Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_Webb "Aston Webb") Building, which is named after one of the architects – the other was [Ingress Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingress_Bell "Ingress Bell"). The initial 25-acre (100,000 m 2) site was given to the university in 1900 by Lord Calthorpe. The grand buildings were an outcome of the £50,000 given by steel magnate and philanthropist [Andrew Carnegie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Carnegie "Andrew Carnegie") to establish a "first class modern scientific college"[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-51) on the model of [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University") in the United States.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-52) Funding was also provided by Sir [Charles Holcroft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holcroft_Baronets "Holcroft Baronets").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-53)

The original domed buildings, built in [Accrington red brick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accrington_brick "Accrington brick"), semicircle to form Chancellor's Court. This sits on a 30 feet (9.1 m) drop, so the architects placed their buildings on two tiers with a 16 feet (4.9 m) drop between them. The clock tower stands in the centre of the Court.

The campanile itself draws its inspiration from the [Torre del Mangia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torre_del_Mangia "Torre del Mangia"), a medieval clock tower that forms part of the [Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Pubblico "Palazzo Pubblico") in [Siena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siena "Siena"), Italy.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-54) When it was built, it was described as 'the intellectual beacon of the Midlands' by the _Birmingham Post_. The clock tower was Birmingham's tallest building from the date of its construction in 1908 until 1969; it is now the third highest in the city. It is one of the top 50 tallest buildings in the UK,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-50tallest-55) and the tallest free-standing clock tower in the world,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-CTBUH-14) although there is some confusion about its actual height, with the university listing it both as 110 metres (361 ft)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Tour-56) and 325 feet (99 m) tall in different sources.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Trail-57)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Old_Joe_Big.jpg/250px-Old_Joe_Big.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Old_Joe_Big.jpg)

Old Joe, the university's [clock tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clock_tower "Clock tower"), remains the tallest freestanding clock tower in the world.

The campus has a wide diversity in architectural types and architects. "What makes Birmingham so exceptional among the Red Brick universities is the deployment of so many other major Modernist practices: only Oxford and Cambridge boast greater selections".[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-58) The Guild of Students original section was designed by Birmingham inter-war architect [Holland Hobbiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holland_W._Hobbiss "Holland W. Hobbiss") who also designed the [King Edward's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Edward's_School,_Birmingham "King Edward's School, Birmingham") opposite. It was described as "Redbrick Tudorish" by [Nikolaus Pevsner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolaus_Pevsner "Nikolaus Pevsner").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-59)

The statue on horseback fronting the entrance to the university and [Barber Institute of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barber_Institute_of_Fine_Arts "Barber Institute of Fine Arts") is a 1722 statue of [George I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_I_of_Great_Britain "George I of Great Britain") rescued from Dublin in 1937. This was saved by Bodkin, a director of the National Gallery of Ireland and first director of the Barber Institute. The statue was commissioned by the [Dublin Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin_Corporation "Dublin Corporation") from the Flemish sculptor [John van Nost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_van_Nost "John van Nost").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-60)

Final negotiations for part of what is now the Vale were completed in only March 1947. By then, properties that would have their names used for halls of residences, such as Wyddrington and Maple Bank, were under discussion and more land was obtained from the Calthorpe estate in 1948 and 1949, providing the setting for the Vale.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-61) Landscape architect [Mary Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Mitchell_(landscape_architect) "Mary Mitchell (landscape architect)") designed the layout of the campus and she included mature trees that were retained from the former gardens.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-listedplan-62) Construction on the Vale started in 1962 with the creation of a 3-acre (12,000 m 2) artificial lake and the building of Ridge, High, Wyddrington and Lake Halls. The first, Ridge Hall, opened for 139 women in January 1964, with its counterpart High Hall admitting its first male residents the following October.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-63)

#### 1960s and modern expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 1960s and modern expansion")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/49/Learning_Center.jpg/250px-Learning_Center.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Learning_Center.jpg)

The university's Learning Centre (left), School of Computer Science (right) and Sir [Eduardo Paolozzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eduardo_Paolozzi "Eduardo Paolozzi")'s Faraday sculpture

The university underwent a major expansion in the 1960s owing to the production of a masterplan by [Casson, Conder and Partners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casson,_Conder_and_Partners "Casson, Conder and Partners").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The first of the major buildings to be constructed to a design by the firm was the Refectory and Staff House, which was built in 1961 and 1962. The two buildings are connected by a bridge. The next major buildings to be constructed were the Wyddrington and Lake Halls and the Faculty of Commerce and Social Science, all completed in 1965.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The Faculty of Commerce and Social Science, now known as the Ashley Building, was designed by Howell, Killick, Partridge and Amis and is a long, curving two-storey block linked to a five-storey [whorl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiral "Spiral"). The two-storey block follows the curve of the road, and has load-bearing brick cross walls. It is faced in specially-made concrete blocks. The spiral is faced with faceted pre-cast concrete cladding panels.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-hickman-25) It was [statutorily listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building") in 1993[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-STS-64) and a refurbishment by Berman Guedes Stretton was completed in 2006.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-65)

[Chamberlin, Powell and Bon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamberlin,_Powell_and_Bon "Chamberlin, Powell and Bon") were commissioned to design the Physical Education Centre, which was built in 1966. The main characteristic of the building is the roof of the changing rooms and small gymnasium, which has hyperbolic paraboloid roof light shells and is completely paved in quarry tiles. The roof of the sports hall consists of eight conoidal 2½-inch thick sprayed concrete shells springing from 80-foot (24 m) long pre-stressed valley beams. On the south elevation, the roof is supported on raking pre-cast columns and reversed shells form a [cantilevered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantilever "Cantilever") canopy.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Also completed in 1966 was the Mining and Minerals Engineering and Physical Metallurgy Departments, which was designed by [Philip Dowson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Dowson "Philip Dowson") of [Arup Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arup_Group "Arup Group"). This complex consisted of four similar three-storey blocks linked at the corners. The frame is of pre-cast reinforced concrete with columns in groups of four and the whole is planned as a tartan grid, allowing services to be carried vertically and horizontally so that at no point in a room are services more than ten feet away. The building received the 1966 [RIBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Institute_of_British_Architects "Royal Institute of British Architects") Architecture Award for the West Midlands.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-hickman-25) It was [statutorily listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building") in 1993.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-STS-64) Taking the full five years from 1962 to 1967, Birmingham erected twelve buildings, which each cost in excess of a quarter of a million pounds.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-66)

[![Image 20](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/40/University_of_Birmingham_-_geograph.org.uk_-_464655.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Birmingham_-_geograph.org.uk_-_464655.jpg)

Faculty of Arts Building

In 1967, Lucas House, a new hall of residence designed by [The John Madin Design Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Madin "John Madin"), was completed, providing 150 study bedrooms. It was constructed in the garden of a large house. The Medical School was extended in 1967 to a design by Leonard J. Multon and Partners. The two-storey building was part of a complex that covers the southside of [Metchley Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metchley_Fort "Metchley Fort"), a Roman fort. In 1968, the Institute for Education in the Department for Education was opened. This was another Casson, Conder and Partners-designed building. The complex consisted of a group of buildings centred around an eight-storey block, containing study offices, laboratories and teaching rooms. The building has a reinforced concrete frame that is exposed internally, and the external walls are of silver-grey rustic bricks. The roofs of the lecture halls, penthouse and Child Study wing are covered in copper.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-hickman-25)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Muirhead_Tower_at_University_of_Birmingham.jpg/250px-Muirhead_Tower_at_University_of_Birmingham.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Muirhead_Tower_at_University_of_Birmingham.jpg)

Muirhead tower, as viewed from near The Bratby Bar

Arup Associates returned in the 1960s to design the Arts and Commerce Building, better known as Muirhead Tower and houses the Institute of Local Government Studies. This was completed in 1969.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-hickman-25) A£42 million refurbishment of the 16-storey tower was completed in 2009 and it now houses the Colleges of Social Sciences and the Cadbury Research Library, the new home for the university's Special Collections. The podium was remodeled around the existing Allardyce Nicol studio theatre, providing additional rehearsal spaces and changing and technical facilities. The ground floor lobby now incorporates a [Starbucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starbucks "Starbucks") coffee shop.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Reisz-67) The name, Muirhead Tower, came from that of the first philosophy professor of the university [John Henry Muirhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Henry_Muirhead "John Henry Muirhead").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Reisz-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-69)

Completed in 2012, the Bramall Music Building is a 450-seat concert hall, which completes the redbrick semicircle of the Aston Webb building, designed by [Glenn Howells Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Howells_Architects "Glenn Howells Architects") with venue design by Acoustic Dimensions. This auditorium, with its associated research, teaching and rehearsal facilities, houses the Department of Music.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-70)

In August 2011 the university announced a £175 million investment in transforming the campus, including a flagship new library and indoor sports centre.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-71) The new main library was constructed on a site adjacent to the old library, which was demolished and replaced by the 'Green Heart' open space. This demolition restored an iconic 1930s sightline from the North Gate to the clock tower.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-72) The sports centre was developed by architects [Lifschutz Davidson Sandilands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifschutz_Davidson_Sandilands "Lifschutz Davidson Sandilands") and [S&P](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_&_Poor's "Standard & Poor's"), and opened in 2017. Its membership is open to the general public.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-73)

The Teaching and Learning building, a subject-agnostic building providing new state-of-the-art lecture theatres and seminar rooms, was constructed on the plot immediately north of the new library and opened in January 2020. In 1978, University station, on the [Cross-City Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-City_Line "Cross-City Line"), was opened to serve the university and its hospital. It is the only university campus in mainland Britain with its own railway station.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 2021, construction began on a redeveloped facility adjacent to the existing structure as part of the West Midlands Rail Programme (WMRP).[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-:0-75) The rebuilt station was completed and opened to the public in January 2024.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-76) Nearby, the Steampipe Bridge, which was constructed in 2011, transports steam across the Cross-City Railway Line and [Worcester & Birmingham Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worcester_and_Birmingham_Canal "Worcester and Birmingham Canal") from the energy generation plant to the medical school as part of the university's sustainable energy strategy. Its laser-cut exterior is also a public art feature.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-77)

#### Other features

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Other features")]

Located within the Edgbaston site of the university is the [Winterbourne Botanic Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winterbourne_Botanic_Garden "Winterbourne Botanic Garden"), a 24,000-square-metre (258,000 square foot) [Edwardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwardian_period "Edwardian period")[Arts and Crafts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_and_Crafts "Arts and Crafts")-style garden. The large statue in the foreground was a gift to the university by its sculptor Sir Edward Paolozzi – the sculpture is named "Faraday", and has an excerpt from the poem _[The Dry Salvages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dry\_Salvages "The Dry Salvages")_ by [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot "T. S. Eliot") around its base.

The University of Birmingham operates the [Lapworth Museum of Geology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapworth_Museum_of_Geology "Lapworth Museum of Geology") in the Aston Webb Building in [Edgbaston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgbaston "Edgbaston"). It is named after [Charles Lapworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lapworth "Charles Lapworth"), a geologist who worked at Mason Science College.

Since November 2007, the university has been holding a [farmers' market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmers'_market "Farmers' market") on the campus.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-78) Birmingham is the first university in the country to have an accredited farmers' market.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-79)

The considerable extent of the estate meant that by the end of the 1990s it was valued at £536 million.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-autogenerated1-80)

University of Birmingham marked its grand ending of Green Heart Project at the start of 2019.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-82)

In 2021, the University opened a central-city meeting and conference site called _The Exchange_ in the former [Birmingham Municipal Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Municipal_Bank "Birmingham Municipal Bank") in [Centenary Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centenary_Square "Centenary Square").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-83)

### Selly Oak campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Selly Oak campus")]

The university's [Selly Oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selly_Oak "Selly Oak") campus is a short distance to the south of the main campus. It was the home of a federation of nine colleges, known as [Selly Oak Colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selly_Oak_Colleges "Selly Oak Colleges"), mainly focused on theology, social work, and teacher training.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-84) The Federation was for many years associated with the University of Birmingham. A new library, the Orchard Learning Resource Centre, was opened in 2001, shortly before the Federation ceased to exist. The OLRC is now one of the University of Birmingham's site libraries.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-85) Among the [Selly Oak Colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selly_Oak_Colleges "Selly Oak Colleges") was Westhill College, (later the University of Birmingham, Westhill), which merged with the university's School of Education in 2001.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-86) In the following years most of the remaining colleges closed, leaving two colleges which continue today, [Woodbrooke College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodbrooke_College "Woodbrooke College"), a study and conference centre for the [Society of Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Friends "Society of Friends"), and [Fircroft College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fircroft_College "Fircroft College"), a small adult education college with residential provision. [Woodbrooke College's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodbrooke_Quaker_Study_Centre "Woodbrooke Quaker Study Centre") Centre for Postgraduate Quaker Studies, established in 1998, works with the University of Birmingham to deliver research supervision for the degrees of MA by research and PhD.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-87)

The Selly Oak campus is now home to the Department of Drama and Theatre Arts in the newly refurbished [Selly Oak Colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selly_Oak_Colleges "Selly Oak Colleges") Old Library and George Cadbury Hall 200-seat theatre.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-88) The UK [daytime television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytime_television "Daytime television") show _[Doctors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctors\_(2000\_TV\_series) "Doctors (2000 TV series)")_ is filmed on this campus.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-89) The [University of Birmingham School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham_School "University of Birmingham School") occupies a brand new, purpose-built building located on the university's Selly Oak campus.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-90) The [University of Birmingham School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham_School "University of Birmingham School") is sponsored by the University of Birmingham and managed by an Academy Trust. The [University of Birmingham School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham_School "University of Birmingham School") opened in September 2015.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-91)

### Mason College and Queen's College campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Mason College and Queen's College campus")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Mason_Science_College.png/250px-Mason_Science_College.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mason_Science_College.png)

The [Mason College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mason_Science_College "Mason Science College") building housed the Faculties of Arts and Law until 1962 (picture date: 1880)

The Victorian neo-gothic [Mason College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mason_College "Mason College") Building in Birmingham city centre housed the University of Birmingham's Faculties of Arts and Law for more than 50 years after the founding of the university in 1900. The Faculty of Arts building on the Edgbaston campus was not constructed until 1959–61. The Faculties of Arts and Law then moved to the Edgbaston campus.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-92) The original [Mason College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mason_College "Mason College") Building was demolished in 1962 as part of the redevelopment within the inner ring road.

The 1843 Gothic Revival building constructed opposite the Town Hall between Paradise Street (the main entrance) and Swallow Street served as [Queen's College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_College,_Birmingham "Queen's College, Birmingham"), one of the founder colleges of the university. In 1904 the building was given a new buff-coloured terracotta and brick front. The medical and scientific departments merged with Mason College in 1900 to form the University of Birmingham and sought new premises in Edgbaston. The theological department of Queen's College did not merge with Mason College, but later moved in 1923 to Somerset Road in Edgbaston, next to the University of Birmingham as the [Queen's Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Queen's_Foundation "The Queen's Foundation"), maintaining a relationship with the University of Birmingham until a 2010 review. In the mid 1970s, the original Queen's College building was demolished, with the exception of the grade II listed façade.

### Academic departments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Academic departments")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Aston_webb1.JPG/250px-Aston_webb1.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aston_webb1.JPG)

Stained glass window in the Great Hall

Birmingham has departments covering a wide range of subjects. On 1 August 2008, the university's system was restructured into five 'colleges', which are composed of numerous 'schools':

*   **Arts and Law** (English, Drama and Creative Studies; History and Cultures; Languages, Cultures, Art History and Music; Liberal Arts, Birmingham Law School; Philosophy, Theology and Religion)
*   **Engineering and Physical Sciences** (Chemistry; Chemical Engineering; Computer Science; Engineering (comprising the Departments of civil, Mechanical and Electrical, Electronic & Systems Engineering); Mathematics; Metallurgy and Materials; Physics and Astronomy)
*   **Life and Environmental Sciences** (Biosciences; Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences; Psychology; Sport and Exercise Sciences)
*   **Medicine and Health** (Institute of Cancer and Genomic Sciences; Institute of Clinical Sciences; Institute of Inflammation and Ageing; Institute of Applied Health Research; Institute of Cardiovascular Science; Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy; Institute of Metabolism and Systems Research; Institute of Microbiology and Infection).
*   **Social Sciences** ([Birmingham Business School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Business_School_(University_of_Birmingham) "Birmingham Business School (University of Birmingham)"); Education; Government and Society; Social Policy)

The university is home to a number of research centres and schools, including the Birmingham Business School, the oldest business school in England, the [University of Birmingham Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham_Medical_School "University of Birmingham Medical School"), the International Development Department, the Institute of Local Government Studies, the [Centre of West African Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_of_West_African_Studies "Centre of West African Studies"), the Centre for Russian and East European Studies, the Centre of Excellence for Research in Computational Intelligence and Applications and the [Shakespeare Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare_Institute "Shakespeare Institute"). The [Third Sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voluntary_sector "Voluntary sector") Research Centre was established in 2008,[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-94) and the Institute for Research into [Superdiversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superdiversity "Superdiversity") was established in 2013.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-95) Apart from traditional research and PhDs, under the department of Engineering and Physical Sciences, the university offers split-site PhD in Computer Science.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-:74-96) The university is also home to the [Birmingham Solar Oscillations Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Solar_Oscillations_Network "Birmingham Solar Oscillations Network") (BiSON) which consists of a network of six remote solar observatories monitoring low-degree solar oscillation modes. It is operated by the High Resolution Optical Spectroscopy group of the School of Physics and Astronomy, funded by the [Science and Technology Facilities Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_and_Technology_Facilities_Council "Science and Technology Facilities Council") (STFC).[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-97)

The university also offer programmes through the Birmingham International Academy (BIA), which supports students with integrated foundation years and Presessional English courses to prepare for university study.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-98)

#### International Development Department

The International Development Department (IDD) is a multi-disciplinary academic department focused on [poverty reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_reduction "Poverty reduction") through developing effective governance systems. #### University of Birmingham Observatory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: University of Birmingham Observatory")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/UoBirmingham_Observatory.jpg/250px-UoBirmingham_Observatory.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UoBirmingham_Observatory.jpg)

The University of Birmingham Astronomical Observatory

In the early 1980s, the University of Birmingham constructed an observatory next to the university playing fields, approximately 5 miles (8.0 km) south of the Edgbaston campus. The site was chosen because the night sky was ~100 times darker than the skies above campus. First light was on 8 December 1982, and the Observatory was officially opened by the [Astronomer Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomer_Royal "Astronomer Royal"), [Francis Graham-Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Graham-Smith "Francis Graham-Smith"), on 13 June 1984.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-103) The observatory was upgraded in 2013.

The Observatory is used primarily for undergraduate teaching.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-104) It has two main instruments, a 16" [Cassegrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassegrain_reflector "Cassegrain reflector") (working at f/19) and a 14" [Meade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meade_Instruments "Meade Instruments") LX200R (working at f/6.35). A third telescope is also present and is used exclusively for visual observations.

Members of the public are given chance to visit the Observatory at regular _Astronomy in the City_ events during the winter months.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-105) These events include a talk on the night sky from a member of the university's student [Astronomical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham_Guild_of_Students "University of Birmingham Guild of Students"); a talk on current astrophysics research, such as [exoplanets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exoplanet "Exoplanet"), [galaxy clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_cluster "Galaxy cluster") or [gravitational-wave astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational-wave_astronomy "Gravitational-wave astronomy"),[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-106) a question-and-answer session, and the chance to observing using telescopes both on campus and at the Observatory.

### Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Finances")]

In the financial year ending 31 July 2024, Birmingham had a total income of £926 million (2022/23 – £909.1 million) and total expenditure of £726.5 million (2022/23 – £884.7 million).[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Birmingham_Financial_Statement_23/24-107) Key sources of income included £456.3 million from tuition fees and education contracts (2022/23 – £445.1 million), £109.5 million from funding body grants (2022/23 – £112.9 million), £205.2 million from research grants and contracts (2022/23 – £196.7 million), £13.4 million from investment income (2022/23 – £9.8 million) and £9.3 million from donations and endowments (2022/23 – £9.6 million).[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Birmingham_Financial_Statement_23/24-107)

At year end, Birmingham had endowments of £155.8 million (2022/23 – £142.5 million) and total net assets of £1.310 billion (2022/23 – £1.106 billion). It holds the [eleventh-largest endowment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UK_universities_by_endowment "List of UK universities by endowment") of any university in the UK.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Birmingham_Financial_Statement_23/24-107)

### Libraries and collections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Birmingham&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Libraries and collections")]

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Bham-library.jpg/250px-Bham-library.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bham-library.jpg)

The old main library, which has now been demolished

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/University_of_Birmingham._Main_Library_%2833445558518%29.jpg/250px-University_of_Birmingham._Main_Library_%2833445558518%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Birmingham._Main_Library_(33445558518).jpg)

The Main Library opened in 2016

Library Services operates six libraries. They are the Barber Fine Art Library, Barnes Library, Main Library, Orchard Learning Resource Centre, Dental Library, and the Shakespeare Institute Library. Library Services also operates the Cadbury Research Library.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-108)

The Shakespeare Institute's library is a major United Kingdom resource for the study of English Renaissance literature.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-109)

The Cadbury Research Library is home to the University of Birmingham's historic collections of rare books, manuscripts, archives, photographs and associated artefacts. The collections, which have been built up over a period of 120 years consist of more than 200,000 rare printed books including significant [incunabula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incunabula "Incunabula"), as well as more than 4 million unique archive and manuscript collections.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-110) The Cadbury Research Library is responsible for directly supporting the university's research, learning and teaching agenda, along with supporting the national and international research community.

The Cadbury Research Library contains the Chamberlain collection of papers from [Neville Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Chamberlain "Neville Chamberlain"), [Joseph Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Chamberlain "Joseph Chamberlain") and [Austen Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austen_Chamberlain "Austen Chamberlain"), the Avon Papers belonging to [Anthony Eden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Eden "Anthony Eden") with material on the [Suez Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez_Crisis "Suez Crisis"), the Cadbury Papers relating to the [Cadbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadbury_Schweppes "Cadbury Schweppes") firm from 1900 to 1960, the Mingana Collection of Middle Eastern Manuscripts of [Alphonse Mingana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Mingana "Alphonse Mingana"), the [Noël Coward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No%C3%ABl_Coward "Noël Coward") Collection, the papers of [Edward Elgar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Elgar "Edward Elgar"), [Oswald Mosley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oswald_Mosley "Oswald Mosley"), [Allardyce Nicoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allardyce_Nicoll "Allardyce Nicoll") and [David Lodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lodge_(author) "David Lodge (author)"), and the records of the English [YMCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YMCA "YMCA") and of the [Church Missionary Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Missionary_Society "Church Missionary Society"). The Cadbury Research Library has recently taken in the complete archive of UK [Save the Children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Save_the_Children "Save the Children"). The Library holds important first editions such as De Humani Corporis (1543) by Versalius, the Complete Works (1616) of Ben Jonson, two copies of The Temple of Flora (1799-1807) by Robert Thornton and comprehensive collections of the works of [Joseph Priestley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Priestley "Joseph Priestley") and [D H Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D_H_Lawrence "D H Lawrence") as well as many other significant works.

In 2015, [a Quranic manuscript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Quran_manuscript "Birmingham Quran manuscript") in the Mingana Collection was identified as one of the oldest to have survived, having been written between 568 and 645.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-UoB-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-BBC-33436021-112)

At the beginning of the 2016/17 academic year, a new main library opened on the Edgbaston campus and the old library has now been demolished as part of the plans to create a 'Green Heart' as per the original plans for the university whereby the clock tower would be visible from the North Gate.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-113)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-114) The Harding Law Library was closed and renovated to become the university's Translation and Interpreting Suite.

### Medicine

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/BirminghamQueenElizabethHospitalMedicalSchool.jpg/250px-BirminghamQueenElizabethHospitalMedicalSchool.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BirminghamQueenElizabethHospitalMedicalSchool.jpg)

The [Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham_Medical_School "University of Birmingham Medical School")

The University of Birmingham's medical school is one of the largest in Europe with more than 450 medical students being trained in each clinical year and more than 1,000 teaching, research, technical and administrative staff [_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]. The school has [centres of excellence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_of_excellence "Center of excellence") in cancer, pharmacy, [immunology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunology "Immunology"), cardiovascular disease, [neuroscience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroscience "Neuroscience") and [endocrinology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endocrinology "Endocrinology"), and is renowned internationally for its research and developments in these fields.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-115)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] The medical school has close links with the [NHS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_Service_(England) "National Health Service (England)") and works closely with 15 teaching hospitals and 50 primary care training practices in the [West Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_(county) "West Midlands (county)").

The [University Hospital Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Hospital_Birmingham_NHS_Foundation_Trust "University Hospital Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust") is the main teaching hospital in the West Midlands. In 2026, Birmingham was ranked 12th in the UK and 63rd in the world universities ranking by [_Time_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)") magazine and [Statista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statista "Statista").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-123) The 2022 _U.S. News & World Report_ ranks the university 91st in the world.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-124) In 2019, it is ranked 137th among the universities around the world by _[SCImago Institutions Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SCImago\_Institutions\_Rankings "SCImago Institutions Rankings")_.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-125)

In 2021 the Times Higher Education placed Birmingham 12th in the UK.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-126) In 2013, Birmingham was named "[_Sunday Times_ University of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday_Times_University_of_the_Year "Sunday Times University of the Year") 2014".[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-THE2014-127) The 2013 [QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QS_World_University_Rankings "QS World University Rankings") placed the University of Birmingham 10th in the UK and 62nd internationally. Birmingham was ranked 12th in the UK in the 2008 [Research Assessment Exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Assessment_Exercise "Research Assessment Exercise") with 16 per cent of the university's research regarded as world-leading and 41 per cent as internationally excellent, with particular strengths in the fields of music, physics, biosciences, computer science, mechanical engineering, political science, international relations and law.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-128)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-129)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Times_profile-130)

In 2015 the Complete University Guide placed Birmingham 5th in the UK for graduate prospects.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-131)

Data from the _[Higher Education Funding Council for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher\_Education\_Funding\_Council\_for\_England "Higher Education Funding Council for England")_ (HEFCE) placed the university amongst the twelve elite institutions who among them take more than half of the students with the highest A-level grades.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-telegraph-132)

Birmingham traditionally had a focus on science, engineering, commerce and coal mining, but has now expanded its provision. It hosted the first [Cancer Research UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer_Research_UK "Cancer Research UK") Centre,[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-133) and making notable contributions to [gravitational-wave astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational-wave_astronomy "Gravitational-wave astronomy"), hosting the Institute of Gravitational Wave Astronomy.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-134)

The Department of Philosophy ranked 3rd in the 2017 Guardian University League Tables.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-135) The combined course of Computer Science and Information Systems, titled Computer Systems Engineering was ranked 4th in the 2016 Guardian University guide.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-136)

In the 2024/25 academic year, the student body consisted of 40,025 students, composed of 25,530 undergraduates and 14,500 postgraduate students.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-HESA_citation-8) The university is consistently designated as a 'high-tariff' institution by the [Department for Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Education "Department for Education"), with the average undergraduate entrant to the university in recent years amassing between 145–152 [UCAS Tariff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCAS_Tariff "UCAS Tariff") points in their top three pre-university qualifications – the equivalent of AAA to A*AA at [A-Level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-level_(United_Kingdom) "A-level (United Kingdom)").[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-Mean_Tariff-142) Based on 2022/23 [HESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_Education_Statistics_Agency "Higher Education Statistics Agency") entry standards data published in domestic league tables, which include a broad range of qualifications beyond the top three exam grades, the average student at the University of Birmingham achieved 161 points – the 24th highest in the country.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-CUG_Entry-140) In 2016, the university gave offers of admission to 79.2% of applicants, the 8th highest amongst the Russell Group.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-149) In 2022, offers were given to 61.3% of undergraduate applicants, the 30th lowest offer rate across the country.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-150)

According to the 2017 _Times_ and _Sunday Times_ Good University Guide, approximately 20% of Birmingham's undergraduates come from independent schools.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-151) In the 2016–17 academic year, the university had a domicile breakdown of 76:5:18 of UK:EU:non-EU students respectively, with a female to male ratio of 56:44.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-152) 50.3% of [international students](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_students_in_the_United_Kingdom "International students in the United Kingdom") enrolled at the institution are from China, the fourth highest proportion out of all mainstream universities in the UK.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Birmingham#cite_note-153)
