Immediately to the north-west of the city centre is [Leazes Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leazes_Park "Leazes Park"), first opened to the public in 1873[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-87) after a petition by 3,000 working men of the city for "ready access to some open ground for the purpose of health and recreation". Just outside one corner of this is [St James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James'_Park "St James' Park"), the stadium home of [Newcastle United FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_United_FC "Newcastle United FC") which dominates the view of the city from all directions.

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/St_James_Park_Newcastle_as_seen_from_south_of_the_River_Tyne.jpg/500px-St_James_Park_Newcastle_as_seen_from_south_of_the_River_Tyne.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_James_Park_Newcastle_as_seen_from_south_of_the_River_Tyne.jpg)

View of [St James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James'_Park "St James' Park") on the skyline and surrounding buildings, as seen from Gateshead

Another major [green space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_belt "Green belt") in the city is the [Town Moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_Moor,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Town Moor, Newcastle upon Tyne"), lying immediately north of the city centre. It is larger than London's [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_London "Hyde Park, London") and [Hampstead Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampstead_Heath "Hampstead Heath") put together[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo1-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo2-89) and the [freemen of the city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City") have the right to graze cattle on it.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo1-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-townmoo2-89) The right extends to the pitch of [St. James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._James'_Park "St. James' Park"), [Newcastle United Football Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_United "Newcastle United")'s ground; this is not exercised, although the Freemen do collect rent for the loss of privilege. Honorary freemen include [Bob Geldof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Geldof "Bob Geldof"),[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-BobGeldof2010-09-17-90)[King Harald V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Harald_V "King Harald V") of Norway,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-KingHNorway-91)[Bobby Robson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Robson "Bobby Robson"),[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-SirBobby2010-09-17-92)[Alan Shearer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Shearer "Alan Shearer"),[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-AlanShearer2010-09-17-93) the late [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela")[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Mandela2010-09-17-94) and the [Royal Shakespeare Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Shakespeare_Company "Royal Shakespeare Company").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-RoyalShakespeare-95)[The Hoppings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hoppings "The Hoppings") funfair, said to be the largest [travelling funfair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travelling_funfair "Travelling funfair") in Europe, is held here annually in June.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Hop2010-09-17-96)

In the south-eastern corner of the Town Moor is [Exhibition Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exhibition_Park,_Newcastle "Exhibition Park, Newcastle"), which contains the only remaining pavilion from the [North East Coast Exhibition of 1929](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Coast_Exhibition "North East Coast Exhibition"). From the 1970s until 2006, this housed the Newcastle Military Vehicle Museum; which closed in 2006. The pavilion is now being used as a [microbrewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microbrewery "Microbrewery") and concert venue for [Wylam Brewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wylam_Brewery "Wylam Brewery").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-97)

### Ouseburn

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Ouseburn")]

The wooded gorge of the [Ouseburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouseburn "Ouseburn") in the east of the city is known as [Jesmond Dene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesmond_Dene "Jesmond Dene") and forms another recreation area, linked by Armstrong Park and Heaton Park to the [Ouseburn Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouseburn_Valley "Ouseburn Valley"), where the river finally reaches the [River Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne,_England "River Tyne, England").

The springtime [dawn chorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_chorus_(birds) "Dawn chorus (birds)") at 55 degrees latitude has been described as one of the best in the world.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-dawnChorus-98) The dawn chorus of the Jesmond Dene green space has been professionally recorded and has been used in various workplace and hospital rehabilitation facilities.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-dawnChorus-98)

### Quayside

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Quayside")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Quayside%2C_Newcastle_upon_Tyne.jpg/250px-Quayside%2C_Newcastle_upon_Tyne.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Quayside,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne.jpg)

Quayside architecture, showing the historic [Newcastle Guildhall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guildhall,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Guildhall, Newcastle upon Tyne") with its white turret

The area around the [Tyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tyne "River Tyne") Gorge, between Newcastle on the north bank and [Gateshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead "Gateshead") on the south bank, is the famous Newcastle-Gateshead [Quayside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quayside "Quayside"). It is famed for its series of dramatic bridges, including the [Tyne Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyne_Bridge "Tyne Bridge") of 1928 which was built by [Dorman Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorman_Long "Dorman Long") of [Middlesbrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesbrough "Middlesbrough"), [Robert Stephenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stephenson "Robert Stephenson")'s [High Level Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Level_Bridge,_River_Tyne "High Level Bridge, River Tyne") of 1849, the first road/rail bridge in the world, and the [Swing Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_Bridge,_River_Tyne "Swing Bridge, River Tyne") of 1876.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-99)

Large-scale [regeneration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_renewal "Urban renewal") efforts have led to the replacement of former shipping premises with new office developments; a tilting bridge - the [Gateshead Millennium Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateshead_Millennium_Bridge "Gateshead Millennium Bridge") - integrated the Quayside more closely with the Gateshead Quayside, home to the [BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BALTIC_Centre_for_Contemporary_Art "BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art") (the venue for the [Turner Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turner_Prize "Turner Prize") 2011)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-TurnerPrize2010-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-101) and the [Norman Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Foster,_Baron_Foster_of_Thames_Bank "Norman Foster, Baron Foster of Thames Bank")-designed [Glasshouse International Centre for Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasshouse_International_Centre_for_Music "Glasshouse International Centre for Music"). The Newcastle and Gateshead Quaysides are now a cosmopolitan area with bars, restaurants, hotels and public spaces.

### Grainger Town

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Grainger Town")]

Main article: [Grainger Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Town "Grainger Town")

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b1/Newcastle_England%2C_Grainger_Street_c._1906.jpg/250px-Newcastle_England%2C_Grainger_Street_c._1906.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Newcastle_England,_Grainger_Street_c._1906.jpg)

Grainger Street, circa 1906

The historic heart of Newcastle is the Grainger Town area. Established on classical streets built by [Richard Grainger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Grainger "Richard Grainger"), a builder and developer, between 1835 and 1842, some of Newcastle upon Tyne's finest buildings and streets lie within this area of the city centre including [Grainger Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Market "Grainger Market"), [Theatre Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_Royal,_Newcastle "Theatre Royal, Newcastle"), [Grey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_grey "Earl grey") Street, Grainger Street and [Clayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Clayton_(town_clerk) "John Clayton (town clerk)") Street.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) These buildings are predominantly four stories high, with vertical dormers, domes, turrets and spikes. Richard Grainger was said to 'have found Newcastle of bricks and timber and left it in stone'.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) Of Grainger Town's 450 buildings, 244 are [listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"), of which 29 are grade I and 49 are grade II*.

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Earl_Grey_atop_his_monument_%28geograph_2368405%29.jpg/250px-Earl_Grey_atop_his_monument_%28geograph_2368405%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Earl_Grey_atop_his_monument_(geograph_2368405).jpg)

Grey's Monument

[Grey's Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's_Monument "Grey's Monument"), which commemorates Prime Minister [Earl Grey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Grey,_2nd_Earl_Grey "Charles Grey, 2nd Earl Grey") and his [Reform Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Act_1832 "Reform Act 1832") of 1832, stands above [Monument Metro station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_metro_station "Monument metro station") and was designed and built by [Edward Hodges Baily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hodges_Baily "Edward Hodges Baily") and [Benjamin Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_and_Benjamin_Green "John and Benjamin Green"). Hodges, who also built [Nelson's Column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson's_Column "Nelson's Column"), designed and built the statue,[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Baily2010-2010-07-26-104) and the monument plinth was designed and built by Benjamin Green.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-BenjaminGreen2010-07-26-105)

The Grainger Market replaced an earlier market originally built in 1808 called the Butcher Market.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Grain201308-106) The Grainger Market was Newcastle's first indoor market.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) At the time of its opening in 1835, it was said to be one of the largest and most beautiful markets in Europe.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) The opening was celebrated with a grand dinner attended by 2000 guests, and the Laing Art Gallery has a painting of this event.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) With the exception of the timber roof which was destroyed by a fire in 1901 and replaced by latticed-steel arches the Market is largely in its original condition.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-ggrmrkt2-103) The Grainger Market architecture, like most in Grainger Town, which are either grade I or II listed, was listed grade I in 1954 by English Heritage.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Grain201308-106)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-107)

The development of the city in the 1960s saw the demolition of part of [Grainger Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grainger_Town "Grainger Town") as a prelude to the modernist rebuilding initiatives of [T. Dan Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._Dan_Smith "T. Dan Smith"), the leader of [Newcastle City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_City_Council "Newcastle City Council"). A corruption scandal was uncovered involving Smith and [John Poulson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Poulson "John Poulson"), a [property developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate_developer "Real estate developer") from [Pontefract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontefract "Pontefract"), West Yorkshire, and both were imprisoned. Echoes of the scandal were revisited in the late 1990s in the [BBC TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_TV "BBC TV") series, _[Our Friends in the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our\_Friends\_in\_the\_North "Our Friends in the North")_.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-108)

### Housing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Housing")]

The [Tyneside flat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyneside_flat "Tyneside flat") was the dominant housing form constructed at the time when the industrial centres on Tyneside were growing most rapidly. They can still be found in areas such as South Heaton in Newcastle but once dominated the streetscape on both sides of the Tyne.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-110) Tyneside flats were built as terraces, one of each pair of doors led to an upstairs flat while the other led into the ground-floor flat, each of two or three rooms. A new development in the Ouseburn valley has recreated them; Architects Cany Ash and Robert Sakula were attracted by the possibilities of high density without building high and getting rid of common areas.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-111)

In terms of housing stock, the authority is one of few authorities to see the proportion of detached homes rise in the 2010 Census (to 7.8%), in this instance this was coupled with a similar rise in flats and waterside apartments to 25.6%, and the proportion of converted or shared houses in 2011 renders this dwelling type within the highest of the five colour-coded brackets at 5.9%, and on a par with [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford") and [Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading,_Berkshire "Reading, Berkshire"), greater than [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") and [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool "Liverpool") and below a handful of historic densely occupied, arguably overinflated markets in the local authorities: [Harrogate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrogate "Harrogate"), [Cheltenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheltenham "Cheltenham"), [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath,_Somerset "Bath, Somerset"), inner London, [Hastings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastings "Hastings"), [Brighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton "Brighton") and [Royal Tunbridge Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Tunbridge_Wells "Royal Tunbridge Wells").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-112)

Significant Newcastle [housing developments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_developments "Housing developments") include [Ralph Erskine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Erskine_(architect) "Ralph Erskine (architect)")'s the [Byker Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byker_Wall "Byker Wall") designed in the 1960s, and now [Grade II* listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"). It is on [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s list of outstanding 20th-century buildings.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-113) The Byker Redevelopment has won the first [Veronica Rudge Green Prize in Urban Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veronica_Rudge_Green_Prize_in_Urban_Design "Veronica Rudge Green Prize in Urban Design") in 1988.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-114)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Climate")]

Newcastle has an [oceanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate") climate ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): _[Cfb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic\_climate "Oceanic climate")_). Data in Newcastle was first collected in 1802 by the solicitor [James Losh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Losh "James Losh").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-tyneWeather1800s-115) Situated in the [rain shadow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_shadow "Rain shadow") of the [North Pennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pennines "North Pennines"), Newcastle is amongst the driest cities in the UK. Temperature extremes recorded at Newcastle Weather Centre include 37.0°C (98.6°F) set on 19 July 2022[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-116) down to −14.0°C (6.8°F) on 29 December 1995.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-117) Newcastle can have cool to cold winters, though usually milder than the rural areas around it, and summers range from pleasant to fairly warm, with very long daylight hours in comparison to all other major English cities. Newcastle upon Tyne shares the same latitude as [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen"), southern Sweden and [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow").

Unlike more western, windward areas of the British Isles affected by heavy rain (that tends to be concentrated in the cooler months), Newcastle has less seasonal variation in rainfall, and less rainfall overall, compared to the UK average. Snowfall is not the norm and often light. Despite snowfall becoming even less frequent due to the effects of [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), Newcastle nevertheless receives more than most major English cities, with any given year averaging 5-10 days of lying snow.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-118)

The nearest weather station to provide sunshine statistics is at Durham, about 14 miles (23 km) south of [Newcastle City Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_City_Centre "Newcastle City Centre"). Durham's inland, less urbanised setting results in night-time temperature data about 1 degree cooler than Newcastle proper throughout the year.

### Environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Environment")]

Main article: [North East Green Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Green_Belt "North East Green Belt")

The city is located within the centre of the North East Green Belt, also known as the Tyne and Wear Green Belt.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-122)

The green belts stated aims[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-123) are to:

*   _Prevent the merging of settlements_
*   _Safeguard the countryside from encroachment_
*   _Check unrestricted [urban sprawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban\_sprawl "Urban sprawl")_
*   _Assist in urban regeneration in the city-region by encouraging the recycling of derelict and other urban land_

The green belt surrounds [Brunswick Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick_Village "Brunswick Village"), [Dinnington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinnington,_Tyne_and_Wear "Dinnington, Tyne and Wear"), Callerton, [Hazlerigg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazlerigg "Hazlerigg"), [Throckley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Throckley "Throckley"), [Walbottle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walbottle "Walbottle"), and [Woolsington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolsington "Woolsington"). Popular locations such as Ryton Island, Tyne Riverside Country Park, the city's golf courses, [Newcastle Racecourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_Racecourse "Newcastle Racecourse"), and [Newcastle International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_International_Airport "Newcastle International Airport") fall inside the green belt.

The city has been recognised for its commitment to environmental issues, with a programme planned for Newcastle to become "the first [carbon neutral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_neutrality "Carbon neutrality") city"[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-124) however, those plans have been revised and they now hope to be carbon neutral by 2050.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-125)

## Culture

### Nightlife

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_upon_Tyne&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Nightlife")]

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/The_Gate_Newcastle.jpg/250px-The_Gate_Newcastle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Gate_Newcastle.jpg)

The Gate complex on Newgate Street is a nightlife destination.

In 2006, _The [Rough Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough\_Guides "Rough Guides") to Britain_ placed Newcastle upon Tyne's nightlife as Great Britain's number one [tourist attraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourist_attraction "Tourist attraction").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-rGuideNo1NLife-126) In 2010, the [Tripadvisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripadvisor "Tripadvisor") Travellers' Choice Destination Awards for Nightlife destinations, Newcastle was awarded third place in Europe (behind [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") and [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"))[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-tripadvisor2010-08-12-127) and seventh place in the world.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-Tripadvisor2-2010-08-12-128) In July 2023, Newcastle was voted the best city in the UK for food, fashion and nightlife.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-vibesJuly2023-129)

There are many bars on the [Bigg Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bigg_Market "Bigg Market") and its adjoining streets. Other areas popular for nightlife include Collingwood Street (commonly referred to as the 'Diamond Strip' due to its concentration of high-end bars). Neville Street, the [Central Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_railway_station "Newcastle railway station") area, Osborne Road in [Jesmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesmond "Jesmond") and the wider [Ouseburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouseburn "Ouseburn") area are home to a variety of younger metropolitan bars. In 1967, London based [Smith's Crisps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Smith's_Snackfood_Company "The Smith's Snackfood Company") created Salt & Vinegar flavour crisps which were first produced by their Newcastle based subsidiary [Tudor Crisps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudor_Crisps "Tudor Crisps") and tested in Tudor's home market of north-east England before being launched nationally.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne#cite_note-134)

The **University of Newcastle upon Tyne**, which [trades as](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_name "Trading name")**Newcastle University**,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-8) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") based in Newcastle upon Tyne, [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"). It has overseas campuses in Singapore and Malaysia. The university is a [red brick university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_brick_university "Red brick university") and a founding member of the Russell Group,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-9) an association of research-intensive UK universities.

The university's history began with the School of Medicine and Surgery (later the College of Medicine), established in Newcastle in 1834, and the [College of Physical Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Fenwick_Boyd#College_of_Physical_Science "Edward Fenwick Boyd") (later renamed Armstrong College), founded in 1871. These two colleges came to form the larger division of the federal [University of Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Durham "University of Durham"), with the [Durham Colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleges_of_Durham_University "Colleges of Durham University") forming the other. The Newcastle colleges merged to form **King's College** in 1937. In 1963, following an act of Parliament, King's College became the University of Newcastle upon Tyne.

The university is subdivided into three faculties: the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences; the Faculty of Medical Sciences; and the Faculty of Science, Agriculture and Engineering. The university offers over 200 full-time undergraduate degree programmes and over 300 postgraduate taught and research programmes across a range of disciplines.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-10) The annual income of the institution for 2024–25 was £618.7 million of which £133.8 million was from research grants and contracts, with an expenditure of £621 million.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-Newcastle_Financial_Statement_24/25-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Armstrong_Building%2C_Newcastle_University%2C_7_September_2013_%2814%29.jpg/250px-Armstrong_Building%2C_Newcastle_University%2C_7_September_2013_%2814%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Armstrong_Building,_Newcastle_University,_7_September_2013_(14).jpg)

The Armstrong Building

See also: [History of Durham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Durham_University "History of Durham University") and [Colleges of Durham University §Colleges in Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleges_of_Durham_University#Colleges_in_Newcastle "Colleges of Durham University")

The establishment of a university in Newcastle upon Tyne was first proposed in 1831 by [Thomas Greenhow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Michael_Greenhow "Thomas Michael Greenhow") in a lecture to the [Literary and Philosophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_and_Philosophical_Society "Literary and Philosophical Society"). In 1832 a group of local medics – physicians George Fife (teaching _materia medica_ and therapeutics) and Samuel Knott (teaching theory and practice of medicine), and surgeons [John Fife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fife_(surgeon) "John Fife (surgeon)") (teaching surgery), Alexander Fraser (teaching anatomy and physiology) and Henry Glassford Potter (teaching chemistry) – started offering medical lectures in Bell's Court to supplement the apprenticeship system (a fourth surgeon, Duncan McAllum, is mentioned by some sources among the founders, but was not included in the prospectus). The first session started on 1 October 1832 with eight or nine students, including [John Snow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Snow "John Snow"), then apprenticed to a local surgeon-apothecary, the opening lecture being delivered by John Fife. In 1834 the lectures and practical demonstrations moved to the Hall of the Company of Barber Surgeons to accommodate the growing number of students, and the School of Medicine and Surgery was formally established on 1 October 1834.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-13)

Architecture Building, Newcastle University

On 25 June 1851, following a dispute among the teaching staff, the school was formally dissolved and the lecturers split into two rival institutions. The majority formed the Newcastle College of Medicine, and the others established themselves as the Newcastle upon Tyne College of Medicine and Practical Science with competing lecture courses.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-14) In July 1851 the majority college was recognised by the [Society of Apothecaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Apothecaries "Society of Apothecaries") and in October by the [Royal College of Surgeons of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_College_of_Surgeons_of_England "Royal College of Surgeons of England") and in January 1852 was approved by the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London") to submit its students for London medical degree examinations. Later in 1852, the majority college was formally linked to the [University of Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_University "Durham University"), becoming the "Newcastle-upon-Tyne College of Medicine in connection with the University of Durham".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-15) The college awarded its first 'Licence in Medicine' (LicMed) under the auspices of the University of Durham in 1856, with external examiners from Oxford and London, becoming the first medical examining body in the United Kingdom to institute practical examinations alongside written and _viva voce_ examinations. The two colleges amalgamated in 1857, with the first session of the unified college opening on 3 October that year.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-16) In 1861 the degree of Master of Surgery was introduced, allowing for the double qualification of Licence of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery, along with the degrees of Bachelor of Medicine and Doctor of Medicine, both of which required residence in Durham. In 1870 the college was brought into closer connection with the university, becoming the "Durham University College of Medicine" with the Reader in Medicine becoming the Professor of Medicine, the college gaining a representative on the university's senate, and residence at the college henceforth counting as residence in the university towards degrees in medicine and surgery, removing the need for students to spend a period of residence in Durham before they could receive the higher degrees.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-17)

Attempts to realise a place for the teaching of sciences in the city were finally met with the foundation of the [College of Physical Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Fenwick_Boyd#College_of_Physical_Science "Edward Fenwick Boyd") in 1871. The college offered instruction in mathematics, physics, chemistry and geology to meet the growing needs of the mining industry, becoming the "Durham College of Physical Science" in 1883 and then renamed after [William George Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_George_Armstrong,_1st_Baron_Armstrong "William George Armstrong, 1st Baron Armstrong") as _Armstrong College_ in 1904. Both of these institutions were part of the University of Durham, which became a federal university under the [University of Durham Act 1908](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Durham_Act_1908 "University of Durham Act 1908") ([8 Edw. 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8_Edw._7 "8 Edw. 7"). c. 20) with two divisions in Durham and Newcastle. By 1908, the Newcastle division was teaching a full range of subjects in the Faculties of Medicine, Arts, and Science, which also included agriculture and engineering.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-18)

Throughout the early 20th century, the medical and science colleges outpaced the growth of their Durham counterparts. Following tensions between the two Newcastle colleges in the early 1930s, a [royal commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_commission "Royal commission") in 1934 recommended the merger of the two colleges to form "King's College, Durham"; that was effected by the [University of Durham Act 1935](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Durham_Act_1935 "University of Durham Act 1935") ([25 & 26 Geo. 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25_&_26_Geo._5 "25 & 26 Geo. 5"). c. 29). Further growth of both division of the federal university led to tensions within the structure and a feeling that it was too large to manage as a single body. On 1 August 1963 the **Universities of Durham and Newcastle upon Tyne Act 1963** (c. xi) separated the two thus creating the "University of Newcastle upon Tyne".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-19) As the successor of King's College, Durham, the university at its founding in 1963, adopted the [coat of arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms "Coat of arms") originally granted to the Council of King's College in 1937.

Above the [portico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portico "Portico") of the Students' Union building are bas-relief carvings of the arms and mottoes of the University of Durham, Armstrong College and Durham University College of Medicine, the predecessor parts of Newcastle University. While a Latin motto, _mens agitat molem_ (_mind moves matter_) appears in the Students' Union building, the university itself does not have an official motto.

In 1967, Newcastle became the only British university to confer an honorary degree on [Martin Luther King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King "Martin Luther King").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-20)

The university established a branch campus in London in 2015, in partnership with [INTO University Partnerships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INTO_University_Partnerships "INTO University Partnerships"), at INTO's existing London campus.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-21) The London campus was closed in 2021.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-22)

In 2024, Newcastle University had a drop in income of £35 million, referred to as a crisis by the local branch of the [Universities and Colleges Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_and_Colleges_Union "Universities and Colleges Union") (UCU). The university had already made £15 million of savings in its budget for the year, but this left a deficit of £20 million.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-23) As a result, academic promotions were cancelled and the university announced a voluntary redundancy scheme.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-24) The UCU held a consultative ballot of members on possible strike action related to the cuts in November 2024.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-25)

The university occupies a campus site close to [Haymarket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_Haymarket "Newcastle Haymarket") in central Newcastle upon Tyne. It is located to the northwest of the city centre between the open spaces of [Leazes Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leazes_Park "Leazes Park") and the [Town Moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_Moor,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Town Moor, Newcastle upon Tyne"); the university medical school and [Royal Victoria Infirmary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Victoria_Infirmary "Royal Victoria Infirmary") are adjacent to the west.

The Armstrong building is the oldest building on the campus and is the site of the original Armstrong College. The building was constructed in three stages;[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-26) the north east wing was completed first at a cost of £18,000 and opened by [Princess Louise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Louise,_Duchess_of_Argyll "Princess Louise, Duchess of Argyll") on 5 November 1888. The south-east wing, which includes the Jubilee Tower, and south-west wings were opened in 1894. The Jubilee Tower was built with surplus funds raised from an Exhibition to mark [Queen Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria "Queen Victoria")'s [Jubilee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Jubilee "Golden Jubilee") in 1887. The north-west front, forming the main entrance, was completed in 1906 and features two stone figures to represent science and the arts. Much of the later construction work was financed by Sir Isaac [Lowthian Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowthian_Bell "Lowthian Bell"), the [metallurgist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallurgy "Metallurgy") and former [Lord Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mayor "Lord Mayor") of Newcastle, after whom the main tower is named. In 1906 it was opened by [King Edward VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Edward_VII "King Edward VII").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-royalopen-27)

The building contains the _King's Hall_, which serves as the university's chief hall for ceremonial purposes where [Congregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graduation "Graduation") ceremonies are held. It can contain 500 seats.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-28) King Edward VII gave permission to call the Great Hall, King's Hall.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-royalopen-27) During the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), the building was requisitioned by the [War Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Office "War Office") to create the first Northern General Hospital, a facility for the [Royal Army Medical Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Army_Medical_Corps "Royal Army Medical Corps") to treat military casualties.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-30) Graduation photographs are often taken in the University Quadrangle, next to the Armstrong building. In 1949 the Quadrangle was turned into a formal garden in memory of members of Newcastle University who gave their lives in the two World Wars.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-31) In 2017, a statue of [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.") was erected in the inner courtyard of the Armstrong Building, to celebrate the 50th anniversary of his honorary degree from the university.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-32)

The Bruce Building is a former brewery, constructed between 1896 and 1900 on the site of the Hotspur Hotel, and designed by the architect [Joseph Oswald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Oswald "Joseph Oswald")[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-Pearson1999-33) as the new premises of [Newcastle Breweries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_Breweries "Newcastle Breweries") Limited.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-35) The university occupied the building from the 1950s, but, having been empty for some time, the building was refurbished in 2016 to become residential and office space.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-37)

The Devonshire Building

The Devonshire Building, opened in 2004, incorporates in an energy efficient design. It uses [photovoltaic cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic_cell "Photovoltaic cell") to help to power motorised shades that control the temperature of the building and [geothermal heating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geothermal_heating "Geothermal heating") coils. Its architects won awards in the Hadrian awards and the [RICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Institution_of_Chartered_Surveyors "Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors") Building of the Year Award 2004. The university won a [Green Gown Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Gown_Awards "Green Gown Awards") for its construction.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-Devonshire_Building_-_The_Hadrian_Awards-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-Accolade_for_Devonshire_Building-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-Devonshire_Building_praised_by_HEFCE-40)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Kings_Gate_building.jpg/250px-Kings_Gate_building.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kings_Gate_building.jpg)

The King's Gate building hosts student and administrative services and was built in 2009.

Plans for additions and improvements to the campus were made public in March 2008 and completed in 2010 at a cost of £200 million. They included a redevelopment of the south-east (Haymarket) façade with a five-storey King's Gate administration building as well as new student accommodation. Two additional buildings for the school of medicine were also built.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-2010plans-41) September 2012 saw the completion of the new buildings and facilities for [INTO Newcastle University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INTO_University_Partnerships "INTO University Partnerships") on the university campus. The main building provides 18 new teaching rooms, a Learning Resource Centre, a lecture theatre, science lab, administrative and academic offices and restaurant.

The Philip Robinson Library is the main university library and is named after a bookseller in the city and benefactor to the library. The Walton Library specialises in services for the Faculty of Medical Sciences in the Medical School. It is named after [Lord Walton of Detchant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron_Walton_of_Detchant "Baron Walton of Detchant"), former Dean of the Faculty of Medicine and Professor of Neurology. The library has a relationship with the Northern region of the [NHS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_Service_(England) "National Health Service (England)") allowing their staff to use the library for research and study. The Law Library specialises in resources relating to law, and the Marjorie Robinson Library Rooms offers additional study spaces and computers. Together, these house over one million books and 500,000 electronic resources. Some schools within the university, such as the School of Modern Languages, also have their own smaller libraries with smaller highly specialised collections.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-42)

In addition to the city centre campus there are buildings such as the [Dove Marine Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dove_Marine_Laboratory "Dove Marine Laboratory") located on [Cullercoats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cullercoats "Cullercoats") Bay,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-43) and Cockle Park Farm in [Northumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland "Northumberland").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-44)

Leazes Terrace, a Grade I listed building, designed by [Thomas Oliver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Oliver_(architect) "Thomas Oliver (architect)") and built by [Richard Grainger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Grainger "Richard Grainger"), in 1829–34; now student accommodation.

Newcastle University has many catered and non-catered [halls of residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halls_of_residence "Halls of residence") available to first-year students, located around the city of Newcastle.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-47) Popular Newcastle areas for private student houses and flats off campus include [Jesmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesmond "Jesmond"), [Heaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaton,_Newcastle "Heaton, Newcastle"), [Sandyford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandyford,_Newcastle_upon_Tyne "Sandyford, Newcastle upon Tyne"), [Shieldfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shieldfield "Shieldfield"), [South Shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shields "South Shields") and [Spital Tongues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spital_Tongues "Spital Tongues").

[Henderson Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henderson_Hall,_Newcastle "Henderson Hall, Newcastle") was used as a hall of residence but "had been empty for a few years" before a fire destroyed it in 2023.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-48)

St Mary's College in [Fenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenham "Fenham"), one of the halls of residence, was formerly St Mary's College of Education, a teacher training college.

## Organisation and governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Organisation and governance")]

The current [chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education) "Chancellor (education)") is the British poet and artist [Imtiaz Dharker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imtiaz_Dharker "Imtiaz Dharker"). She assumed the position of chancellor on 1 January 2020.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-Imtaizncl-49) The vice-chancellor is [Chris Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Day_(hepatologist) "Chris Day (hepatologist)"), a hepatologist and former pro-vice-chancellor of the faculty of medical sciences.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-50)

The university has an enrolment of some 16,000 undergraduate and 5,600 postgraduate students. Teaching and research are delivered in 19 academic schools,[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-51) 13 research institutes and 38 research centres, spread across three faculties: the faculty of humanities and social sciences; the faculty of medical sciences; and the faculty of science, agriculture and engineering.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-52) The university offers around 175 full-time undergraduate degree programmes in a wide range of subject areas spanning arts, sciences, engineering and medicine, together with approximately 340 postgraduate taught and research programmes across a range of disciplines.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-structure-53)

It holds a series of public lectures called 'Insights' each year in the Curtis Auditorium in the Herschel Building. Many of the university's partnerships with companies, like [Red Hat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hat "Red Hat"), are housed in the Herschel Annex.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-54)[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]

### Civic responsibility

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Civic responsibility")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Old_Quad%2C_Newcastle_University%2C_5_September_2013.jpg/250px-Old_Quad%2C_Newcastle_University%2C_5_September_2013.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Old_Quad,_Newcastle_University,_5_September_2013.jpg)

The university Quadrangle

The university describes itself as a civic university,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-55) with a role to play in society by bringing its research to bear on issues faced by communities (local, national or international).

In 2012, the university opened the Newcastle Institute for Social Renewal[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-56) to address issues of social and economic change, representing the research-led academic schools across the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-57) and the Business School.

[Mark Shucksmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shucksmith "Mark Shucksmith") was Director of the Newcastle Institute for Social Renewal (NISR) at Newcastle University, where he is also Professor of Planning.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-58)

In 2006, the university was granted [fair trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_trade "Fair trade") status and from January 2007 it became a [smoke-free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoke-free "Smoke-free") campus.

The university has also been actively involved with several of the region's museums for many years. The [Great North Museum: Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Museum:_Hancock "Great North Museum: Hancock") originally opened in 1884 and is often a venue for the university's events programme.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-59)

Newcastle University Business School

As early as the 1900/1 academic year, there was teaching in [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") ([political economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_economy "Political economy"), as it was then known) at Newcastle, making Economics the oldest department in what would only much later become the Business School.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-60) The Economics Department is currently headed by the [Sir David Dale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_David_Dale,_1st_Baronet "Sir David Dale, 1st Baronet") Chair.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-61) Among the eminent economists having served in the Department (both as holders of the Sir David Dale Chair) are [Harry Mainwaring Hallsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1931_Birthday_Honours "1931 Birthday Honours") and [Stanley Dennison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_R._Dennison "Stanley R. Dennison").

#### Business School

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Business School")]

Like its peers in the north of England, such as the business schools of [University of Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bradford "University of Bradford") and [Manchester Metropolitan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Metropolitan_University "Manchester Metropolitan University"), Newcastle University Business School is a [triple accredited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_accreditation "Triple accreditation") business school, with accreditation by the three major accreditation bodies: [AACSB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AACSB "AACSB"), [AMBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_MBAs "Association of MBAs") and [EQUIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EQUIS "EQUIS").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-62)

In 2002, Newcastle University Business School established the Business Accounting and Finance or 'Flying Start' degree in association with the [ICAEW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICAEW "ICAEW") and [PricewaterhouseCoopers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PricewaterhouseCoopers "PricewaterhouseCoopers").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-fly-63) The course offers an accelerated route towards the [ACA Chartered Accountancy qualification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Chartered_Accountants_in_England_&_Wales "Institute of Chartered Accountants in England & Wales") and is the Business School's Flagship programme.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-fly-63)

In 2011 the business school opened their new building built on the former [Scottish and Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_and_Newcastle "Scottish and Newcastle") brewery site next to [St James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James'_Park "St James' Park").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-64) This building was officially opened on 19 March 2012 by [Lord Burns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terence_Burns,_Baron_Burns "Terence Burns, Baron Burns").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-65)

The business school operated a central London campus from 2014 to 2021, in partnership with [INTO University Partnerships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INTO_University_Partnerships "INTO University Partnerships") until 2020.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-66)

#### School of Modern Languages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: School of Modern Languages")]

The School of Modern Languages consists of five sections: East Asian (which includes Japanese and Chinese); French; German; Spanish, Portuguese & Latin American Studies; and Translating & Interpreting Studies.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-69) Six languages are taught from beginner's level to full degree level ‒ Chinese, Japanese, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese ‒ and beginner's courses in Catalan, Dutch, Italian and Quechua are also available. Beyond the learning of the languages themselves, Newcastle also places a great deal of emphasis on study and experience of the cultures of the countries where the languages taught are spoken. The School of Modern Languages hosts [North East England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England "North East England")'s only branches of two internationally important institutes: the [Camões Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cam%C3%B5es_Institute "Camões Institute"), a language institute for Portuguese, and the [Confucius Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confucius_Institute "Confucius Institute"), a language and cultural institute for Chinese.

The teaching of modern foreign languages at Newcastle predates the creation of Newcastle University itself, as in 1911 Armstrong College in Newcastle installed [Albert George Latham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_George_Latham "Albert George Latham"), its first professor of modern languages.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-70)

The School of Modern Languages at Newcastle is the lead institution in the North East [Routes into Languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Routes_into_Languages "Routes into Languages") Consortium[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-routeslang-71) and, together with the [Durham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_University "Durham University"), [Northumbria University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumbria_University "Northumbria University"), the [University of Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sunderland "University of Sunderland"), the [Teesside University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teesside_University "Teesside University") and a network of schools, undertakes work activities of discovery of languages for the 9 to 13 years pupils.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-routeslang-71) This implies having festivals, Q&A sessions, language tasters, or quizzes organised, as well as a web learning work aiming at constructing a web portal to link language learners across the region.

Newcastle Law School is the longest established law school in the north-east of England when law was taught at the university's predecessor college before it became independent from Durham University.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-nuls-73) It has a number of recognised international and national experts in a variety of areas of legal scholarship ranging from Common and Chancery law, to International and European law, as well as contextual, socio-legal and theoretical legal studies.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-nuls-73)

The Law School occupies four specially adapted late-Victorian town houses. The Staff Offices, the Alumni Lecture Theatre and seminar rooms as well as the Law Library are all located within the School buildings.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-Undergraduate-74)

#### School of Computing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: School of Computing")]

The School of Computing was ranked in the Times Higher Education world Top 100.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-75) Research areas include Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and ubiquitous computing, secure and resilient systems, synthetic biology, scalable computing (high performance systems, data science, machine learning and data visualization), and advanced modelling. The school led the formation of the National Innovation Centre for Data.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-76) Innovative teaching in the School was recognised in 2017 with the award of a National Teaching Fellowship.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-77)

### Cavitation tunnel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Cavitation tunnel")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/The_Hancock_Museum_Newcastle_September_2009.jpg/250px-The_Hancock_Museum_Newcastle_September_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Hancock_Museum_Newcastle_September_2009.jpg)

The [Hancock Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hancock_Museum "Hancock Museum"), founded in 1884, is the main location of the [Great North Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Museum "Great North Museum").

Newcastle University has the second largest [cavitation tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavitation_tunnel "Cavitation tunnel") in the UK. Founded in 1950, and based in the Marine Science and Technology Department, the [Emerson Cavitation Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson_Cavitation_Tunnel "Emerson Cavitation Tunnel") is used as a test basin for propellers, water turbines, underwater coatings and interaction of propellers with ice.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-78) The Emerson Cavitation Tunnel was recently relocated to a new facility in [Blyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blyth,_Northumberland "Blyth, Northumberland").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-79)

### Museums and galleries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Museums and galleries")]

The university is associated with a number of the region's museums and galleries, including the [Great North Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Museum "Great North Museum") project, which is primarily based at the world-renowned [Hancock Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hancock_Museum "Hancock Museum"). The Great North Museum: Hancock also contains the collections from two of the university's former museums, the [Shefton Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shefton_Museum "Shefton Museum") and the [Museum of Antiquities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Antiquities_(Newcastle_upon_Tyne) "Museum of Antiquities (Newcastle upon Tyne)"), both now closed.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-80) The university's [Hatton Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatton_Gallery "Hatton Gallery") is also a part of the Great North Museum project, and remains within the Fine Art Building.

### Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Finances")]

In the financial year ending 31 July 2024, Newcastle had a total income of £619.8 million (2022/23 – £592.4 million) and total expenditure of £475 million (2022/23 – £558 million).[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-Newcastle_Financial_Statement_23/24-81) Key sources of income included £307.4 million from tuition fees and education contracts (2022/23 – £286.2 million), £88.7 million from funding body grants (2022/23 – £88.9 million), £126.1 million from research grants and contracts (2022/23 – £119.3 million), £9.8 million from investment income (2022/23 – £6 million) and £7.6 million from donations and endowments (2022/23 – £11 million).[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-Newcastle_Financial_Statement_23/24-81)

At year end, Newcastle had endowments of £94.8 million (2023 – £87.1 million) and total net assets of £627.2 million (2023 – £474.9 million). It holds the [sixteenth-largest endowment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UK_universities_by_endowment "List of UK universities by endowment") of any university in the UK.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-Newcastle_Financial_Statement_23/24-81)

Due to a decline in the intake of international students as of 2025, the university is undergoing 300 full-time job cuts to recover from a £35 million shortfall.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-82) Since 20 January 2025, the university heads have proposed a "voluntary severance scheme" to allow staff to voluntarily leave their jobs, but they will not rule out forced job losses if the scheme does not reach their goal. Staff voted to take part in industrial strike action to oppose the cuts.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-83)

In the 2024/25 academic year, the student body consisted of 27,230 students, composed of 21,245 undergraduates and 5,985 postgraduate students.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-HESA_citation-5) The university is consistently designated as a 'high-tariff' institution by the [Department for Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Education "Department for Education"), with the average undergraduate entrant to the university in recent years amassing between 137–143 [UCAS Tariff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCAS_Tariff "UCAS Tariff") points in their top three pre-university qualifications – the equivalent of AAB to AAA at [A-Level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-level_(United_Kingdom) "A-level (United Kingdom)").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-Mean_Tariff-96) Based on 2022/23 [HESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_Education_Statistics_Agency "Higher Education Statistics Agency") entry standards data published in domestic league tables, which include a broad range of qualifications beyond the top three exam grades, the average student at Newcastle University achieved 151 points.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-CUG_Entry-94) In 2015, the university gave offers of admission to 92.1% of its applicants, the highest amongst the Russell Group.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-103)

25.1% of Newcastle's undergraduates are [privately educated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_school_(United_Kingdom) "Independent school (United Kingdom)"), the thirteenth highest proportion amongst mainstream British universities.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-104) In the 2016–17 academic year, the university had a domicile breakdown of 74:5:21 of UK:EU:non-EU students respectively with a female to male ratio of 51:49.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-105)

### Research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Research")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Herschelbuildingnewcastle.jpg/250px-Herschelbuildingnewcastle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Herschelbuildingnewcastle.jpg)

The Herschel Building, home to the School of Mathematics, Statistics and Physics, and several of the university's largest lecture theatres

Newcastle is a member of the Russell Group of 24 research-intensive universities. In the 2021 [Research Excellence Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Excellence_Framework "Research Excellence Framework") (REF), which assesses the quality of research in UK higher education institutions, Newcastle is ranked joint 33rd by GPA (along with the [University of Strathclyde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Strathclyde "University of Strathclyde") and the [University of Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sussex "University of Sussex")) and 15th for research power (the grade point average score of a university, multiplied by the full-time equivalent number of researchers submitted).[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-106)

## Student life

### Students' union

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=35 "Edit section: Students' union")]

Main article: [Newcastle University Students' Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University_Students'_Union "Newcastle University Students' Union")

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Ncle_Union_2012.jpg/250px-Ncle_Union_2012.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ncle_Union_2012.jpg)

Students' Union following refurbishment, 2012

[Newcastle University Students' Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University_Students'_Union "Newcastle University Students' Union") (NUSU), known as the Union Society until a 2012 rebranding, includes student-run sports clubs and societies.

The Union building was built in 1924 following a generous gift from an anonymous donor, who is now believed to have been [Sir Cecil Cochrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Algernon_Cochrane "Cecil Algernon Cochrane"), a major benefactor to the university.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-107) It is built in the neo-[Jacobean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobean_architecture "Jacobean architecture") style and was designed by the local architect [Robert Burns Dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Burns_Dick "Robert Burns Dick"). It was opened on 22 October 1925 by the Rt. Hon. [Lord Eustace Percy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eustace_Percy,_1st_Baron_Percy_of_Newcastle "Eustace Percy, 1st Baron Percy of Newcastle"), who later served as [Rector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rector_(academia) "Rector (academia)") of King's College from 1937 to 1952. It is a Grade II [listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listed_building "Listed building"). In 2010, the university donated £8 million towards a redevelopment project for the Union Building.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-108)

The Students' Union is run by seven paid sabbatical officers, including a Welfare and Equality Officer, and ten part-time unpaid officer positions. The former leader of the Liberal Democrats [Tim Farron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Farron "Tim Farron") was President of NUSU in 1991–1992.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-109) The Students' Union also employs around 300 people in ancillary roles including bar staff and entertainment organisers.

[_The Courier_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Courier_(Newcastle_University_newspaper) "The Courier (Newcastle University newspaper)") is a weekly [student newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_newspaper "Student newspaper"). Established in 1948, the current weekly readership is around 12,000, most of whom are students at the university. _The Courier_ has won _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")'_ s _Student Publication of the Year_ award twice in a row, in 2012 and 2013.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-110) It is published every Monday during term time.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-111)

Newcastle Student Radio is a [student radio station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_radio_station "Student radio station") based in the university. It produces shows on music, news, talk and sport and aims to cater for a wide range of musical tastes.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-112)

NUTV, known as TCTV from 2010 to 2017, is [student television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_television_in_the_United_Kingdom "Student television in the United Kingdom") channel, first established in 2007. It produces live and on-demand content with coverage of events, as well as student-made programmes and shows.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-113)

### Sport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Sport")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Sports_Centre%2C_Newcastle_University%2C_5_September_2013_%281%29.jpg/250px-Sports_Centre%2C_Newcastle_University%2C_5_September_2013_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sports_Centre,_Newcastle_University,_5_September_2013_(1).jpg)

Sports Centre, Newcastle University

Newcastle is one of the leading universities for sport in the UK and is consistently ranked within the top 12 out of 152 higher education institutions in the British Universities and Colleges Sport (BUCS) rankings. More than 50 student-led sports clubs are supported through a team of professional staff and a network of indoor and outdoor sports facilities based over four sites.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-115) The university have a strong rugby history and were the winners of the [Northumberland Senior Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland_senior_cup_rugby_union "Northumberland senior cup rugby union") in 1965.

The university enjoys a friendly sporting rivalry with local universities. The [Stan Calvert Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Calvert_Cup "Stan Calvert Cup")[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-116) was held between 1994 and 2018 by major sports teams from Newcastle and [Northumbria University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumbria_University "Northumbria University"). [The Boat Race of the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Boat_Race_of_the_North "The Boat Race of the North") has also taken place between the [rowing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowing_(sport) "Rowing (sport)") clubs of Newcastle and [Durham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_University "Durham University").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-117)

As of 2026,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Newcastle_University&action=edit)[Newcastle University F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University_F.C. "Newcastle University F.C.") compete in men's senior football in the [Northern League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Football_League "Northern Football League") Division Two.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-118)

The university's [Cochrane Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochrane_Park "Cochrane Park") sports facility was a training venue for the teams playing football games at [St James' Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James'_Park "St James' Park") for the [2012 London Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_London_Olympics "2012 London Olympics").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_University#cite_note-119)
